# Storage and databases {#sec-storage-and-databases}

Every service of the earlier chapters keeps its state somewhere else: the stateless servers of
[The web stack](../the-web-stack/index.qmd) push it into a store, and the queues of
[Performance and queueing](../performance-and-queueing/index.qmd) form in front of one. This chapter is about those
stores on a single machine and the file systems beneath them: how data is modelled, how a schema avoids redundancy, how
indexes and storage engines find a record among millions, what a transaction promises when several clients write at once,
how files, blocks and objects differ, and how a search engine finds the documents that contain a word. Distribution across
machines is left aside; one database is enough to raise every question.

The claims are of two kinds. The data models, normal forms, storage engines, isolation levels, storage services and inverted
indexes are definitions. The results that make them dependable are propositions with complete proofs: Heath's theorem on
lossless decomposition, the height of a B-tree, the false-positive rate of a Bloom filter, and the theorem that a schedule
whose precedence graph has no cycle, in particular every schedule of two-phase locking, is serialisable. One fact of the
Bloom-filter analysis, that the fraction of zero bits concentrates around its mean, needs a martingale argument and is stated as
quoted from its source.

The sources are the benchmark books for the practice, @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Chs. 1 and 6], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024
[Chs. 2 and 4], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Chs. 3, 5 and 11] and @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Chs. 2 and 5, App. 5], and
three section sources, @reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022 [Chs. 5, 6 and 8, App. A],
@pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024 [Ch. 8] and @gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024 [Ch. 13]. Two classic papers
supply the systems: @chang2006bigtable for the wide-column model, SSTables and compactions, and @ghemawat2003google for the
distributed file system. The Bloom-filter analysis follows @broder2004network [Sec. 2.1], and the behaviour of SQLite, which runs
every example, follows its documentation [@sqliteQueryPlanner; @sqliteIsolation; @sqliteFTS5]. The probability comes from
[Probability and statistics](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd).

The chapter has six sections. @sec-data-models defines the data models. @sec-schema-design defines functional dependencies and
normal forms and proves when a decomposition loses nothing. @sec-storage-engines defines indexes, B-trees, LSM trees and Bloom
filters and proves the height of a B-tree and the false-positive rate of a Bloom filter. @sec-transactions defines transactions,
anomalies and isolation levels and proves the serialisability of two-phase locking. @sec-storage-services defines file, block and
object storage and the distributed file system. @sec-full-text-search defines the inverted index and its ranking.

The running example is the metadata of the photo-sharing service (@exm-req-photoshare): users, photos, follows, likes and
captions, with the photos themselves in an object store. Its sizes come from the previous chapters: $2 \times 10^7$ uploads a day,
$1\,\mathrm{kB}$ of metadata per photo (@exm-req-workload-assumptions).

Every definition and proposition is followed by ten examples and ten exercises, each exercise with a hidden solution in two tabs:
the argument, then a computation with its recorded output. The computations run in plain Python 3.12 with NumPy and the standard
library's `sqlite3` (SQLite 3.54), which provides the schemas, query plans, transactions and full-text indexes. Diagrams are
written in the D2 language. Statements specific to other database systems are marked as illustrative and are not run.

## Data models {#sec-data-models}

The first decision about a store is the shape in which it holds data. Xu frames it as a choice "between a traditional
relational database and a non-relational database" and lists when the second "might be the right choice"
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 1, "Which databases to use?"]; Liu warns that "I will use NoSQL because it scales well" is the
kind of answer that "doesn't show deep technical database knowledge" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "How Do I Choose a
Database?"]. The useful question is which operations a model makes cheap. This section defines five models by their data and
their operations, so that a design can match them to its access patterns.

For more on this topic, see @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 5], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Databases"],
@chang2006bigtable [Secs. 2-3] and @pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024 [Ch. 8, "NoSQL databases"].

### Five data models

The models differ in what a stored item is (a row, an opaque value, a document, a cell, a vertex) and in what can be asked of
it without reading everything. The definition states both.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-data-model}
#### Data models

A **data model** is the form in which a store represents data together with the operations it offers on them.

1. **Relational.** Data are relations (tables): sets of tuples (rows) over named attributes (columns) with atomic values. A
   **key** is a set of attributes whose values identify a row. Queries combine relations by selection, projection and **joins**
   on matching attribute values, in SQL, and a transaction may read and write any rows.
2. **Key-value.** Data are a map from keys to values that the store does not interpret. The operations are get, put and delete
   by key, and, if the keys are kept sorted, scans of a key range.
3. **Document.** Data are a map from keys to documents, nested structures such as JSON objects, whose fields the store can
   index and query; documents in one collection need not have the same fields.
4. **Wide-column.** Data are "a sparse, distributed, persistent multidimensional sorted map" indexed by a row key, a column key
   (a column family and a qualifier) and a timestamp, with uninterpreted byte strings as values [@chang2006bigtable, Sec. 2].
   Rows are kept sorted by key, and an operation on one row is atomic.
5. **Graph.** Data are vertices and directed edges, each with properties; queries traverse edges from given vertices.

A design chooses a model by its **access patterns**: the operations it must answer, with their rates and the keys they use.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The relational model is the default of the benchmark books. Xu explains why.

::: {#exm-dm-relational-default}
#### The relational default

"For most developers, relational databases are the best option because they have been around for over 40 years", and a
non-relational one "might be the right choice if" the application needs "super-low latency", the data are "unstructured", it
only needs "to serialize and deserialize data", or it must "store a massive amount of data" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 1,
"Which databases to use?"]. Liu agrees: "you can consider using a relational database unless you find a better reason"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Relational Database"].
:::

The photo service's metadata fits the relational model. Its tables follow the functional requirements.

::: {#exm-dm-photoshare-tables}
#### The photo service in tables

`users(user_id, name, joined)`, `photos(photo_id, owner_id, caption, taken)`, `follows(follower_id, followee_id)` and
`likes(user_id, photo_id)`: each operation of @exm-req-photoshare is a few rows and a join. The feed is "photos whose owner is
followed by me", a join of `follows` and `photos` on the owner.
:::

Sinha and Chopra list the four non-relational families. Each is one item of the definition.

::: {#exm-dm-sinha-families}
#### The non-relational families

"Key-value stores associate a unique key with a data value. They are highly efficient for simple data retrieval but are less
suitable for complex queries"; document databases "store data as documents, such as JSON or XML"; column-family stores "organize
data into column families"; graph databases "use graph structures to represent and navigate relationships between data points"
[@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 5, "NoSQL databases"]. These are items 2 to 5.
:::

A key-value store answers only questions about one key. Liu shows the limit on a schema for file labels.

::: {#exm-dm-key-value-limit}
#### One direction only

Storing labels as `file_id -> [label_id]` answers "give me all the labels associated with the file" efficiently, but "it becomes
tricky with 'give me all the files that belong to a label_id'" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Schema Design"]. A second
map in the other direction answers it, at the price of keeping two maps consistent, which a relational table with an index on
each column does by itself.
:::

The document model suits data whose shape varies. Liu's example is a product catalogue.

::: {#exm-dm-document-catalogue}
#### A product catalogue

A document database fits "a product catalog where the schema between each product catalog could differ significantly", since
"creating a relational table with all the known columns may be wasteful, since the storage will be sparse"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Document Store"]. A camera has a sensor size and a shirt a fabric; each document carries
only its own fields.
:::

Bigtable's Webtable is the wide-column model's standard example. Its row keys are reversed URLs.

::: {#exm-dm-webtable}
#### The Webtable

Webtable uses "URLs as row keys, various aspects of web pages as column names, and store[s] the contents of the web pages in the
contents: column under the timestamps when they were fetched"; the row for `com.cnn.www` has a `contents:` column with three
versions and `anchor:cnnsi.com` and `anchor:my.look.ca` columns [@chang2006bigtable, Sec. 2, Figure 1]. Column families are "the
basic unit of access control", few in number, while "a table may have an unbounded number of columns" (*ibid.*).
:::

Liu's chat schema in a wide-column store puts one conversation in one row. The messages are columns sorted by time.

::: {#exm-dm-chat-wide}
#### Chat in a wide-column store

Liu proposes "Row: chat_id" with columns "message_id, message_text, author_id, created_time", clustered "by created_time since the
typical access pattern of chat is to fetch by timestamp intervals", so that a conversation's messages are "physically next to
each other" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Wide Column Store"]. Reading the latest fifty messages of a chat is one row
and one scan.
:::

Graphs make multi-step relationships cheap to traverse. The follow graph of the photo service is one.

::: {#exm-dm-graph-follows}
#### The follow graph

Users are vertices and follows are edges. "Suggest people followed by the people I follow" is a two-step traversal from one vertex;
in the relational model it is a self-join of `follows`, which an index on `follower_id` makes cheap for two steps but which grows
one join per step. Graph databases "are designed for data with complex relationships" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 5, "NoSQL
databases"].
:::

NoSQL is not a rejection of SQL. Pacheco and Sgro list what it is not.

::: {#exm-dm-pacheco-nosql}
#### What NoSQL is not

NoSQL "is not about replacing relational databases for all its use cases", and it is not "about rejecting SQL. A lot of NoSQL
solutions have SQL-like or full SQL interfaces", nor "about dropping all forms of consistency or durability"
[@pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024, Ch. 8, "NoSQL databases"]. The definition classifies by data and operations, not by
query language.
:::

A system may use several models at once. Gilbert calls it polyglot persistence.

::: {#exm-dm-polyglot}
#### Several models in one system

"Polyglot persistence is the idea that we want to use the right database technology for the work at hand", since "different
database technologies may be better suited for the different data life cycle phases"
[@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 13, "Polyglot persistence"]. The photo service keeps metadata in tables, photos in an
object store and the feed's precomputed pages in a key-value store.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise builds the relational schema of @exm-dm-photoshare-tables in SQLite. The feed is then one query.

::: {#exr-dm-feed-query}
#### The feed as a join

Create the four tables, insert three users, their follows and a few photos, and write the feed of user 1: the photos of the users
it follows, newest first.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The feed joins `follows` (rows with `follower_id = 1`) with `photos` on `owner_id = followee_id` and orders by `taken`. No row
stores the feed itself: it is computed from the facts.

## Python

The schema and the query.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE users(user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE photos(photo_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, owner_id INTEGER REFERENCES users, caption TEXT, taken INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE follows(follower_id INTEGER, followee_id INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id));
CREATE TABLE likes(user_id INTEGER, photo_id INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY (user_id, photo_id));
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'ana'), (2, 'ben'), (3, 'cai');
INSERT INTO follows VALUES (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3);
INSERT INTO photos VALUES (10, 2, 'harbour', 100), (11, 3, 'market', 105), (12, 3, 'night', 110), (13, 1, 'cat', 120);
""")
feed = db.execute("""SELECT p.photo_id, u.name, p.caption FROM follows f JOIN photos p ON p.owner_id = f.followee_id
                     JOIN users u ON u.user_id = p.owner_id WHERE f.follower_id = 1 ORDER BY p.taken DESC""").fetchall()
print(feed)
```

```{.text .run-output}
[(12, 'cai', 'night'), (11, 'cai', 'market'), (10, 'ben', 'harbour')]
```
::::
:::

The second exercise stores the same data as key-value pairs. The cost appears on updates.

::: {#exr-dm-key-value-follows}
#### Follows as values

Store each user's followees as one JSON value under the key `following:<user_id>`. Write the follow operation, and count the bytes
read and written to add one followee for a user who already follows $500$ others with $8$-byte identifiers in JSON. What does the
relational table write instead?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The value is opaque, so a follow reads the whole list, appends and writes it back: about $5\,\mathrm{kB}$ read and written for
$500$ followees of about ten characters each. The table `follows` writes one row of two integers. The key-value layout also makes
two concurrent follows by the same user overwrite each other unless the store offers a conditional write.

## Python

The two layouts.

```{.python .run}
import json
kv = {"following:1": json.dumps([1_000_000_000 + i for i in range(500)])}
def follow(kv, user, other):
    key = f"following:{user}"
    value = json.loads(kv.get(key, "[]"))
    read = len(kv.get(key, ""))
    value.append(other); kv[key] = json.dumps(value)
    return read, len(kv[key])
r, w = follow(kv, 1, 1_000_000_999)
print(f"key-value: read {r} bytes, wrote {w} bytes; relational: one row of 2 integers")
```

```{.text .run-output}
key-value: read 6000 bytes, wrote 6012 bytes; relational: one row of 2 integers
```
::::
:::

The third exercise compares nesting with references in the document model. Comments are the usual case.

::: {#exr-dm-nested-comments}
#### Nested or referenced comments

A photo document embeds its comments as an array. Give the size of the document after $10\,000$ comments of $200$ bytes, and the
bytes rewritten per new comment if the store rewrites whole documents. When should comments be documents of their own?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The document grows to about $2\,\mathrm{MB}$, and each new comment rewrites all of it: the cost per comment grows linearly with the
number of comments. Comments that grow without bound, or that are read separately (the latest twenty), belong in their own
collection keyed by photo and time; embedding suits data that is bounded and always read with its parent, such as a photo's
dimensions.

## Python

The growth.

```{.python .run}
import json
doc = {"photo_id": 10, "caption": "harbour", "comments": []}
for n in (10, 1000, 10_000):
    doc["comments"] = [{"user": 7, "text": "x" * 180} for _ in range(n)]
    print(f"{n:6d} comments: document {len(json.dumps(doc)) / 1e6:.3f} MB rewritten per new comment")
```

```{.text .run-output}
    10 comments: document 0.002 MB rewritten per new comment
  1000 comments: document 0.205 MB rewritten per new comment
 10000 comments: document 2.050 MB rewritten per new comment
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise implements item 4 in a few lines. A sorted map of (row, column, timestamp) to values is enough.

::: {#exr-dm-wide-column}
#### A small Webtable

Store the cells of @exm-dm-webtable in a dictionary keyed by (row, column, timestamp), and write the two reads Bigtable makes
cheap: the latest version of a cell, and all rows in a key range, here all pages of `com.cnn.*`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The latest version is the largest timestamp among the cell's keys; a row range is a scan over the sorted row keys between `com.cnn.`
and the next prefix. Reversed host names make all pages of one domain adjacent, which a URL in its usual order would not.

## Python

The map and the two reads.

```{.python .run}
cells = {("com.cnn.www", "contents:", 3): "<html>v3", ("com.cnn.www", "contents:", 5): "<html>v5",
         ("com.cnn.www", "contents:", 6): "<html>v6", ("com.cnn.www", "anchor:cnnsi.com", 9): "CNN",
         ("com.cnn.www/sport", "contents:", 4): "<html>sport", ("com.example", "contents:", 1): "<html>x"}
latest = max((t, v) for (r, c, t), v in cells.items() if (r, c) == ("com.cnn.www", "contents:"))
rows = sorted({r for (r, c, t) in cells if "com.cnn." <= r < "com.cnn/"})
print("latest contents:", latest); print("rows of com.cnn:", rows)
```

```{.text .run-output}
latest contents: (6, '<html>v6')
rows of com.cnn: ['com.cnn.www', 'com.cnn.www/sport']
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise traverses the follow graph two ways. A recursive SQL query and an adjacency map give the same answer.

::: {#exr-dm-friends-of-friends}
#### Two steps through the graph

For the follow graph `1->2, 1->3, 2->4, 3->4, 3->5, 4->1`, find the users two steps from user 1 that user 1 does not already follow,
with a self-join in SQLite and with an adjacency dictionary.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Two steps from $1$ reach $4$ (via $2$ and $3$) and $5$ (via $3$); user $1$ follows neither, so both are suggested. The self-join
needs one join per step; the adjacency map follows edges directly, which is what a graph store keeps.

## Python

Both computations.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
edges = [(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 4), (3, 5), (4, 1)]
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:"); db.execute("CREATE TABLE follows(a, b)"); db.executemany("INSERT INTO follows VALUES (?, ?)", edges)
sql = db.execute("""SELECT DISTINCT f2.b FROM follows f1 JOIN follows f2 ON f2.a = f1.b
                    WHERE f1.a = 1 AND f2.b <> 1 AND f2.b NOT IN (SELECT b FROM follows WHERE a = 1)""").fetchall()
adj = {}
for a, b in edges:
    adj.setdefault(a, set()).add(b)
two = {c for b in adj[1] for c in adj.get(b, ())} - adj[1] - {1}
print("SQL:", sorted(x for (x,) in sql), "| graph:", sorted(two))
```

```{.text .run-output}
SQL: [4, 5] | graph: [4, 5]
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise measures the row and column layouts of Liu's example. An aggregate over one column reads less in columns.

::: {#exr-dm-row-vs-column}
#### Rows or columns

A table of $10^6$ game sessions has four $8$-byte columns: id, date, hours played and score. Count the bytes read by "average score"
in a row layout and in a column layout, and compress the date column by run-length encoding when the rows are sorted by date with
$1000$ sessions per day, as in Liu's "1:8, 3:5, 2:6" example [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Columnar Store"].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A row layout stores rows contiguously, so scanning one column reads all $32\,\mathrm{MB}$; a column layout reads only the score column,
$8\,\mathrm{MB}$, a quarter. Sorted by date, the date column has $1000$ runs, which run-length encoding stores as $1000$ (value,
count) pairs, $16\,\mathrm{kB}$ instead of $8\,\mathrm{MB}$.

## Python

The byte counts and the encoding.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
n = 10**6
dates = np.repeat(np.arange(1000), 1000)
runs = np.flatnonzero(np.diff(dates)) + 1
print(f"row layout reads {n * 32 / 1e6:.0f} MB, column layout {n * 8 / 1e6:.0f} MB; "
      f"date column: {len(runs) + 1} runs, {16 * (len(runs) + 1) / 1e3:.0f} kB encoded")
```

```{.text .run-output}
row layout reads 32 MB, column layout 8 MB; date column: 1000 runs, 16 kB encoded
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise designs row keys for a wide-column store. The key decides which reads are scans.

::: {#exr-dm-row-keys}
#### Row keys for photos

The photo service stores photo metadata in a wide-column store and must answer "the latest photos of user $u$". Compare the row keys
`photo_id`, `user_id#taken` and `user_id#(max_time - taken)`, and say which makes the query a single short scan.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With `photo_id` a user's photos are scattered. With `user_id#taken` they are adjacent but oldest first, so the latest are at the end
of the range. With the inverted time they are adjacent and newest first: the query is a scan of the first rows of the user's range.
Keys are compared as strings, so the numbers must be zero-padded.

## Python

The three orders for two users.

```{.python .run}
photos = [(101, 7, 1000), (102, 8, 1005), (103, 7, 1010), (104, 7, 1020), (105, 8, 1030)]   # (photo, user, taken)
MAX = 10**10
layouts = {"photo_id": lambda p: f"{p[0]:010d}", "user#taken": lambda p: f"{p[1]:06d}#{p[2]:010d}",
           "user#inverted": lambda p: f"{p[1]:06d}#{MAX - p[2]:010d}"}
for name, key in layouts.items():
    order = [p[0] for p in sorted(photos, key=key)]
    print(f"{name:14s}: {order}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
photo_id      : [101, 102, 103, 104, 105]
user#taken    : [101, 103, 104, 102, 105]
user#inverted : [104, 103, 101, 105, 102]
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise matches models to access patterns. It applies the last paragraph of the definition.

::: {#exr-dm-choose}
#### Choosing models

Choose a model for: (1) sessions looked up by session identifier; (2) orders with line items, payments and refunds that must add up;
(3) sensor readings written at $10^6$ per second and read by sensor and time range; (4) product pages with varying attributes; (5)
"people you may know" two steps away.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(1) key-value: one get by key. (2) relational: multi-row transactions and joins. (3) wide-column: high write rates, rows keyed by
sensor and time for range scans. (4) document: fields vary by product. (5) graph, or a relational table with an index if the
traversal is only two steps.

## Python

The choices as a rule on the dominant operation.

```{.python .run}
patterns = {"sessions": "get by key", "orders": "multi-row transaction", "sensor readings": "range scan, high write rate",
            "product pages": "varying fields", "people you may know": "multi-step traversal"}
model = {"get by key": "key-value", "multi-row transaction": "relational", "range scan, high write rate": "wide-column",
         "varying fields": "document", "multi-step traversal": "graph"}
for k, v in patterns.items():
    print(f"{k:20s}: {v:28s} -> {model[v]}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
sessions            : get by key                   -> key-value
orders              : multi-row transaction        -> relational
sensor readings     : range scan, high write rate  -> wide-column
product pages       : varying fields               -> document
people you may know : multi-step traversal         -> graph
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise examines a claim of Tan's about SQL and NoSQL. Liu says the opposite about ACID.

::: {#exr-dm-acid-claim}
#### Does SQL mean ACID?

Tan writes that a SQL database "must have ACID properties" and that NoSQL is "a database that does not have all SQL properties"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 4.1, p. 78]; Liu writes that "ACID is a very high-level term that isn't necessarily unique to
relational databases", since "it's possible to have transactions on a row or document level in a NoSQL database"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Relational Database"]. Reconcile the two with the definition, using Bigtable's single-row
atomicity as an example.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The definition classifies stores by data and operations; transactions are a further property. Bigtable is not relational, yet "every
read or write of data under a single row key is atomic" [@chang2006bigtable, Sec. 2]: it offers transactions whose scope is one row.
Relational databases usually offer transactions over any rows. Liu is right that ACID guarantees are not unique to the relational
model; Tan's statement is a convention of his book rather than a property of SQL.

## Python

A single-row atomic update in a key-value map, with all of a row's cells changed together under one lock.

```{.python .run}
import threading
table, lock = {"com.cnn.www": {"anchor:a": "x", "anchor:b": "y"}}, threading.Lock()
def apply_row_mutation(row, sets, deletes):
    with lock:                                          # all cells of the row change together
        cells = dict(table.get(row, {}))
        cells.update(sets)
        for c in deletes:
            cells.pop(c, None)
        table[row] = cells
apply_row_mutation("com.cnn.www", {"anchor:www.c-span.org": "CNN"}, ["anchor:a"])
print(table)
```

```{.text .run-output}
{'com.cnn.www': {'anchor:b': 'y', 'anchor:www.c-span.org': 'CNN'}}
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise estimates the size of the photo service's metadata. It decides whether one machine can hold it.

::: {#exr-dm-metadata-size}
#### How much metadata?

With $2 \times 10^7$ photos a day kept for five years at $1\,\mathrm{kB}$ each, $10^8$ users following $200$ others each in rows of
$16$ bytes, and $50$ likes per photo of $16$ bytes, estimate each table's size, ignoring indexes. Which table dominates?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Photos: $3.65 \times 10^{10}$ rows, $36.5\,\mathrm{TB}$. Follows: $2 \times 10^{10}$ rows, $0.32\,\mathrm{TB}$. Likes: $1.8 \times
10^{12}$ rows, $29\,\mathrm{TB}$. Photos and likes dominate; neither fits one machine's disk with room for indexes and replicas, which
is why such tables are split across machines.

## Python

The three sizes.

```{.python .run}
photos = 2e7 * 365 * 5
sizes = {"photos": photos * 1000, "follows": 1e8 * 200 * 16, "likes": photos * 50 * 16}
for k, v in sizes.items():
    print(f"{k:8s}: {v / 1e12:6.2f} TB")
```

```{.text .run-output}
photos  :  36.50 TB
follows :   0.32 TB
likes   :  29.20 TB
```

:::
