The tenth exercise implements B-tree insertion. The invariants of item 2 are checked after every insertion.

::: {#exr-se-btree-insert}
#### Inserting into a B-tree

Implement insertion into a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ by splitting full nodes on the way down, insert $2000$ random keys with $t = 3$,
and check after each insertion that the keys are in order, every non-root node has between $t - 1$ and $2t - 1$ keys and all leaves have
the same depth.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Splitting a full node (with $2t - 1$ keys) before descending into it guarantees that its parent has room for the median. The two halves get
$t - 1$ keys each, so the lower bound holds; the median joins the parent; a split of the root makes a new root with one key and two children,
which is the only way the depth of the leaves changes, and it changes for all leaves at once.

## Python

The insertion with top-down splits, and the invariant check.

```{.python .run}
import random
class Node:
    def __init__(self, keys=None, kids=None):
        self.keys, self.kids = keys or [], kids or []
def split(parent, i, t):
    full = parent.kids[i]
    right = Node(full.keys[t:], full.kids[t:])
    parent.keys.insert(i, full.keys[t - 1]); parent.kids.insert(i + 1, right)
    full.keys, full.kids = full.keys[:t - 1], full.kids[:t]
def insert(root, key, t):
    if len(root.keys) == 2 * t - 1:
        root = Node([], [root]); split(root, 0, t)
    node = root
    while node.kids:
        i = sum(k < key for k in node.keys)
        if len(node.kids[i].keys) == 2 * t - 1:
            split(node, i, t); i += key > node.keys[i]
        node = node.kids[i]
    node.keys.insert(sum(k < key for k in node.keys), key)
    return root
def check(node, t, is_root, depth, depths, out):
    assert (1 if is_root else t - 1) <= len(node.keys) <= 2 * t - 1
    if not node.kids:
        depths.add(depth); out.extend(node.keys); return
    assert len(node.kids) == len(node.keys) + 1
    for j, kid in enumerate(node.kids):
        check(kid, t, False, depth + 1, depths, out)
        if j < len(node.keys):
            out.append(node.keys[j])
random.seed(7)
root, t = Node(), 3
keys = random.sample(range(10**6), 2000)
for n, key in enumerate(keys, 1):
    root = insert(root, key, t)
    depths, out = set(), []
    check(root, t, True, 0, depths, out)
    assert out == sorted(keys[:n]) and len(depths) == 1
print(f"invariants held after each of {len(keys)} insertions; height {depths.pop()}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
invariants held after each of 2000 insertions; height 5
```
::::
:::
::::

### The height of a B-tree

A B-tree lookup reads one node per level, so its cost in page reads is the height plus one. The minimum degree forces every node except the
root to be at least half full, which makes the tree wide and shallow; the proposition turns this into a logarithmic bound.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-btree-height}
#### The height of a B-tree

Let a B-tree of minimum degree $t \geq 2$ hold $n \geq 1$ keys and have height $H$. Then
$$
2t^H - 1 \;\leq\; n \;\leq\; (2t)^{H+1} - 1, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \log_{2t}(n + 1) - 1 \;\leq\; H \;\leq\; \log_t\frac{n + 1}{2},
$$
and a lookup reads at most $H + 1 \leq 1 + \log_t((n+1)/2)$ nodes. Both bounds on $n$ are attained.
:::

::::

*Proof.* For the lower bound, count the nodes at each depth. If $H \geq 1$ the root has at least $2$ children, and every internal node other
than the root has at least $t$ children, so there are at least $2t^{d-1}$ nodes at depth $d$ for $1 \leq d \leq H$. The root holds at least
$1$ key and every other node at least $t - 1$, hence
$$
n \;\geq\; 1 + (t - 1)\sum_{d=1}^{H}2t^{d-1} \;=\; 1 + 2(t - 1)\frac{t^H - 1}{t - 1} \;=\; 2t^H - 1,
$$
which also holds for $H = 0$. For the upper bound, every node has at most $2t$ children, so there are at most $(2t)^d$ nodes at depth $d$,
each with at most $2t - 1$ keys:
$$
n \;\leq\; (2t - 1)\sum_{d=0}^{H}(2t)^d \;=\; (2t)^{H+1} - 1.
$$
Taking logarithms gives the bounds on $H$, and a lookup reads one node at each of the $H + 1$ depths. The lower bound is attained by the tree
whose root has one key and every other node $t - 1$ keys, the upper bound by the tree all of whose nodes have $2t - 1$ keys; both satisfy
item 2 of @def-storage-engine. $\square$

The bound is the reason databases use pages of many keys: with $t$ in the hundreds, $\log_t$ of a billion is about $4$, and the top levels
fit in memory.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A billion keys need few levels. The minimum degree is what matters.

::: {#exm-bt-billion}
#### A billion keys

With $t = 100$ and $n = 10^9$, $H \leq \log_{100}(5 \times 10^8) = 4.35$, so $H \leq 4$ and a lookup reads at most $5$ nodes; with $t = 2$ the
bound is $28.9$, so $H \leq 28$.

```{.python .run}
import math
for t in (2, 100):
    print(f"t = {t:3d}: H <= {math.log((1e9 + 1) / 2, t):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
t =   2: H <= 28.90
t = 100: H <= 4.35
```
:::

The minimum degree comes from the page size. A node is one page.

::: {#exm-bt-page-fanout}
#### Degree from the page size

A page of $4096\,\mathrm{B}$ holding keys of $8\,\mathrm{B}$ and child pointers of $8\,\mathrm{B}$ fits about $4096/16 = 256$ keys, so
$2t - 1 \approx 255$ and $t = 128$; then $10^9$ keys give $H \leq \log_{128}(5 \times 10^8) = 4.1$.
:::

SQLite stores its tables and indexes as B-trees, and its `dbstat` table reports the path of each page. The depth comes out small.

::: {#exm-bt-sqlite-depth}
#### The depth of a SQLite table

The `dbstat` virtual table gives for each page "the path taken from the root node of the btree structure", the root's path being "/"
[@sqliteDbstat, Sec. 2]. SQLite's tables keep the rows in the leaves and only keys in the internal pages, a variant of item 2 in which the
internal nodes have hundreds of children; the run counts the levels for $10^6$ rows.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE photos(photo_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, caption TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO photos VALUES (?, ?)", ((i, f"caption {i}") for i in range(10**6)))
depth, pages, fan = db.execute("""SELECT MAX(LENGTH(path) - LENGTH(REPLACE(path, '/', ''))) - 1, COUNT(*),
    AVG(CASE WHEN pagetype = 'internal' THEN ncell END) FROM dbstat WHERE name = 'photos'""").fetchone()
print(f"height {depth}, pages {pages}, mean keys per internal page {fan:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
height 2, pages 5634, mean keys per internal page 375
```
:::

With $t = 2$ the bounds are tight and easy to list. They show how wide the range of sizes for one height is.

::: {#exm-bt-t2-table}
#### Sizes for each height

For $t = 2$ the proposition gives $2^{H+1} - 1 \leq n \leq 4^{H+1} - 1$: height $0$ holds $1$ to $3$ keys, height $1$ holds $3$ to $15$,
height $2$ holds $7$ to $63$.

```{.python .run}
t = 2
for H in range(5):
    print(f"H = {H}: {2 * t**H - 1} <= n <= {(2 * t)**(H + 1) - 1}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
H = 0: 1 <= n <= 3
H = 1: 3 <= n <= 15
H = 2: 7 <= n <= 63
H = 3: 15 <= n <= 255
H = 4: 31 <= n <= 1023
```
:::

A B-tree beats binary search on disk. Binary search reads one page per comparison.

::: {#exm-bt-vs-binary}
#### Against binary search on pages

Binary search over $10^9$ sorted keys stored on disk makes $\lceil\log_2 10^9\rceil = 30$ comparisons, most on different pages; a B-tree with
$t = 128$ reads at most $5$ pages and does its comparisons within each page in memory. The ratio is about $\log_2 t$.
:::

The top levels are few and small. Caching them removes most reads.

::: {#exm-bt-cached-levels}
#### Caching the top levels

With $t = 128$ and up to $255$ keys per node, depths $0$ to $2$ hold at most $1 + 256 + 256^2 \approx 6.6 \times 10^4$ pages, about
$270\,\mathrm{MB}$ at $4\,\mathrm{kB}$ each; with them in memory a lookup among $10^9$ keys reads at most two pages from disk.
:::

The height grows only when the root splits. Growth is therefore slow.

::: {#exm-bt-growth}
#### Height grows at the root

By the proposition, doubling $n$ raises the upper bound on $H$ by $\log_t 2$, which is $1/7$ for $t = 128$: the tree must grow by a factor of
$t$ before its maximal height grows by one level. The insertion algorithm grows the tree only by splitting the root, which keeps all
leaves at the same depth.
:::

The minimal tree attains the lower bound. It is the sparsest tree item 2 allows.

::: {#exm-bt-minimal}
#### The sparsest tree

For $t = 3$ and $H = 2$ the sparsest tree has a root with $1$ key, $2$ children with $2$ keys each and $6$ leaves with $2$ keys each:
$1 + 4 + 12 = 17 = 2 \cdot 3^2 - 1$ keys.
:::

The full tree attains the upper bound. Every node has $2t - 1$ keys.

::: {#exm-bt-full}
#### The fullest tree

For $t = 3$ and $H = 2$ the full tree has $1 + 6 + 36 = 43$ nodes of $5$ keys, $215 = 6^3 - 1$ keys.
:::

The bound applies to the insertion code of @exr-se-btree-insert. Random insertion lands between the two bounds.

::: {#exm-bt-random-insert}
#### Random insertion

Inserting $2000$ random keys with $t = 3$ gave a tree of height $5$ in @exr-se-btree-insert; the proposition allows
$\log_6 2001 - 1 = 3.24 \leq H \leq \log_3 1000.5 = 6.29$, so $H \in \{4, 5, 6\}$.

```{.python .run}
import math
print(f"{math.log(2001, 6) - 1:.2f} <= H <= {math.log(2001 / 2, 3):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
3.24 <= H <= 6.29
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise inverts the bound. Given a height, how many keys are guaranteed?

::: {#exr-bt-guarantee}
#### Keys per height

A storage engine wants every lookup to read at most $4$ pages, that is $H \leq 3$. With $t = 64$, how many keys can it always store, and how
many can it store at best?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Any tree with $n \leq 2t^4 - 2$ keys has height at most $3$, because height $4$ would need $n \geq 2t^4 - 1$; that is about $3.4 \times 10^7$
keys. At best, full nodes give $(2t)^4 - 1 \approx 2.7 \times 10^8$ keys at height $3$.

## Python

The two numbers.

```{.python .run}
t = 64
print(f"always {2 * t**4 - 2:.3e}, at best {(2 * t)**4 - 1:.3e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
always 3.355e+07, at best 2.684e+08
```
::::
:::

The second exercise proves that the minimal tree is the only tree attaining the lower bound. Equality forces each count.

::: {#exr-bt-equality}
#### When the lower bound is attained

Prove that $n = 2t^H - 1$ holds only if the root has one key and every other node has exactly $t - 1$ keys.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The proof of the proposition bounds $n$ below by a sum of per-node minima over a minimal number of nodes. If any node had more keys than
its minimum, or any depth more nodes than the minimum (which happens if an internal node has more children than its minimum), the sum would be
strictly larger. So equality forces the root to hold one key with two children and every other node $t - 1$ keys.

## Python

The count for the sparsest trees, built level by level.

```{.python .run}
for t in (2, 3, 5):
    for H in range(4):
        nodes, keys = 1, 1
        for d in range(1, H + 1):
            nodes = 2 if d == 1 else nodes * t
            keys += nodes * (t - 1)
        assert keys == 2 * t**H - 1
print("sparsest trees have 2 t^H - 1 keys for t in (2, 3, 5), H < 4")
```

```{.text .run-output}
sparsest trees have 2 t^H - 1 keys for t in (2, 3, 5), H < 4
```
::::
:::

The third exercise measures how full random insertion leaves the nodes. The answer sits between the bounds.

::: {#exr-bt-fill}
#### How full are the nodes?

Using the insertion of @exr-se-btree-insert with $t = 16$, insert $2 \times 10^4$ random keys and $2 \times 10^4$ increasing keys, and report the
height and the mean number of keys per node in each case.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Random keys fill nodes to roughly two thirds of their capacity of $31$. Increasing keys always go into the rightmost leaf, which splits into a
left half that is never touched again, so nodes are left with about $t - 1 = 15$ keys, at the sparse end allowed by item 2. Both heights lie in
the range the proposition allows for $n = 2 \times 10^4$ and $t = 16$, printed on the last line.

## Python

The two insertion orders.

```{.python .run}
import random, math
class Node:
    def __init__(self, keys=None, kids=None):
        self.keys, self.kids = keys or [], kids or []
def split(parent, i, t):
    full = parent.kids[i]
    right = Node(full.keys[t:], full.kids[t:])
    parent.keys.insert(i, full.keys[t - 1]); parent.kids.insert(i + 1, right)
    full.keys, full.kids = full.keys[:t - 1], full.kids[:t]
def insert(root, key, t):
    if len(root.keys) == 2 * t - 1:
        root = Node([], [root]); split(root, 0, t)
    node = root
    while node.kids:
        i = sum(k < key for k in node.keys)
        if len(node.kids[i].keys) == 2 * t - 1:
            split(node, i, t); i += key > node.keys[i]
        node = node.kids[i]
    node.keys.insert(sum(k < key for k in node.keys), key)
    return root
def stats(root):
    nodes, height, level = 0, 0, [root]
    while level:
        nodes += len(level); height += 1
        level = [k for n in level for k in n.kids]
    return height - 1, nodes
random.seed(8)
t, n = 16, 20_000
for name, keys in (("random", random.sample(range(10**7), n)), ("increasing", range(n))):
    root = Node()
    for key in keys:
        root = insert(root, key, t)
    H, nodes = stats(root)
    print(f"{name:10s}: height {H}, mean keys per node {n / nodes:.1f} of at most {2 * t - 1}")
print(f"proposition: {math.log(n + 1, 2 * t) - 1:.2f} <= H <= {math.log((n + 1) / 2, t):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
random    : height 3, mean keys per node 21.5 of at most 31
increasing: height 3, mean keys per node 15.0 of at most 31
proposition: 1.86 <= H <= 3.32
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise counts the pages read by a range query. The leaves of the range are read in order.

::: {#exr-bt-range}
#### Range queries

Prove that an in-order traversal returning the $K$ keys of a range $[\ell, u]$ from a B-tree of height $H$ and minimum degree $t$ reads at most
$(H + 1)(K/(t - 1) + 2)$ nodes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The traversal reads the nodes whose subtree's key interval meets $[\ell, u]$. At a fixed depth these intervals are disjoint and ordered from
left to right, so the nodes read form a contiguous run. Every node of the run other than the first and the last lies between them in key order,
so all its keys are in $[\ell, u]$; it is not the root, so it holds at least $t - 1$ keys of the result. Hence the run has at most
$K/(t - 1) + 2$ nodes, and summing over the $H + 1$ depths gives the bound. The leaves dominate: about one page per $t - 1$ results, which is why
the SQLite documentation counts advancing to the next row as nearly free [@sqliteQueryPlanner, Sec. 1.4].

## Python

The leaf pages a range of $K$ keys touches with $t - 1$ to $2t - 1$ keys per leaf.

```{.python .run}
import math
t = 64
for K in (10, 1000, 100_000):
    print(f"K = {K:6d}: between {math.ceil(K / (2 * t - 1))} and {math.ceil(K / (t - 1)) + 1} leaves")
```

```{.text .run-output}
K =     10: between 1 and 2 leaves
K =   1000: between 8 and 17 leaves
K = 100000: between 788 and 1589 leaves
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise compares a B-tree of degree two with a balanced binary tree. A 2-3-4 tree is the case $t = 2$.

::: {#exr-bt-vs-bst}
#### Degree two

Show that for $t = 2$ the height bound is $H \leq \log_2(n+1) - 1$, compare it with the height of the shortest binary search tree with $n$
keys, and say why a B-tree with large $t$ reads fewer pages when nodes are pages.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With $t = 2$, $\log_t((n+1)/2) = \log_2(n+1) - 1$, which never exceeds $\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil - 1$, the height of the shortest binary search tree
with $n$ keys: even the sparsest 2-3-4 tree is no taller than a perfectly balanced binary tree, and fuller nodes make it shallower. A larger $t$
divides the height by about $\log_2 t$, and with one node per page that is the number of pages read.

## Python

The bounds for a million keys.

```{.python .run}
import math
n = 10**6
print(f"t = 2: H <= {math.log2((n + 1) / 2):.2f}; perfect binary tree {math.ceil(math.log2(n + 1)) - 1}; t = 128: H <= {math.log((n + 1) / 2, 128):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
t = 2: H <= 18.93; perfect binary tree 19; t = 128: H <= 2.70
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise estimates lookup throughput from the height. Uncached levels cost disk reads.

::: {#exr-bt-throughput}
#### Lookups per second

A disk serves $10^4$ random page reads per second. A B-tree of $10^9$ keys with $t = 128$ has its top two levels cached. How many lookups per
second does it sustain at most?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$H \leq 4$, so a lookup reads at most $5$ nodes, of which $2$ are cached and at most $3$ come from disk: at least
$10^4 / 3 \approx 3300$ lookups per second, more when the tree is fuller than the worst case.

## Python

The count.

```{.python .run}
import math
H = math.floor(math.log((1e9 + 1) / 2, 128))
print(f"H <= {H}, disk reads per lookup <= {H + 1 - 2}, lookups/s >= {1e4 / (H + 1 - 2):.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
H <= 4, disk reads per lookup <= 3, lookups/s >= 3333
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise checks the bound against SQLite for growing tables. The run reports the measured height.

::: {#exr-bt-sqlite-growth}
#### Height of SQLite indexes

Build an index on a text column of $10^3$, $10^4$, $10^5$ and $10^6$ random rows and report the height of the index B-tree with `dbstat`, together
with the mean number of keys per internal page.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The height grows by one each time the size grows by a factor comparable to the fan-out, as the proposition says: with about a hundred keys per
internal page, the index has height $1$ up to about ten thousand rows and $2$ at a million.

## Python

The heights.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3, random
random.seed(9)
for n in (10**3, 10**4, 10**5, 10**6):
    db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    db.execute("CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, s TEXT)"); db.execute("CREATE INDEX t_s ON t(s)")
    db.executemany("INSERT INTO t VALUES (?, ?)", ((i, f"{random.getrandbits(48):012x}") for i in range(n)))
    h, fan = db.execute("""SELECT MAX(LENGTH(path) - LENGTH(REPLACE(path, '/', ''))) - 1,
        AVG(CASE WHEN pagetype = 'internal' THEN ncell END) FROM dbstat WHERE name = 't_s'""").fetchone()
    print(f"n = {n:8d}: height {h}, keys per internal page {fan if fan is None else round(fan)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n =     1000: height 1, keys per internal page 5
n =    10000: height 1, keys per internal page 53
n =   100000: height 2, keys per internal page 110
n =  1000000: height 2, keys per internal page 145
```

:::

The eighth exercise proves that a lookup needs at most $H + 1$ node reads. It is the descent of item 2.

::: {#exr-bt-search-correct}
#### Correctness of the descent

Prove that searching for a key $x$ by choosing, at each node, the child between the two keys that bracket $x$ finds $x$ if it is in the tree, after
reading at most $H + 1$ nodes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By the separation property, the keys in the subtree of the $i$-th child lie strictly between the node's $(i-1)$-th and $i$-th keys. If $x$ is
in the subtree of a node and not among its keys, it is in the subtree of the child chosen, so the invariant "$x$ is in the current subtree, if it
is in the tree" holds at every step. Each step goes one level down, and the leaves are at depth $H$, so at most $H + 1$ nodes are read.

## Python

A search on a hand-built tree of height $2$, counting nodes read.

```{.python .run}
import bisect
tree = ([30], [([10, 20], [([5], []), ([15], []), ([25], [])]), ([40], [([35], []), ([45, 50], [])])])
def search(node, x, reads=1):
    keys, kids = node
    i = bisect.bisect_left(keys, x)
    if i < len(keys) and keys[i] == x:
        return True, reads
    return (False, reads) if not kids else search(kids[i], x, reads + 1)
print({x: search(tree, x) for x in (30, 15, 50, 12)})
```

```{.text .run-output}
{30: (True, 1), 15: (True, 3), 50: (True, 3), 12: (False, 3)}
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise relates the height bound to the size of the keys. Long keys mean small fan-out.

::: {#exr-bt-key-size}
#### Long keys

With $4096$-byte pages and $8$-byte pointers, compare the height bound for $10^9$ keys of $8$ bytes and of $120$ bytes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Keys of $8$ bytes give about $256$ keys per page, $t = 128$ and $H \leq 4$; keys of $120$ bytes give $32$ per page, $t = 16$ and
$H \leq \log_{16}(5 \times 10^8) = 7.2$, so $H \leq 7$. Short keys, or prefixes of keys in internal nodes, keep the tree shallow.

## Python

Both bounds.

```{.python .run}
import math
for key in (8, 120):
    t = (4096 // (key + 8) + 1) // 2
    print(f"key {key:3d} B: t = {t}, H <= {math.floor(math.log((1e9 + 1) / 2, t))}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
key   8 B: t = 128, H <= 4
key 120 B: t = 16, H <= 7
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise checks both bounds of the proposition on random trees. The insertion of @exr-se-btree-insert supplies them.

::: {#exr-bt-check-bounds}
#### The bounds on random trees

For $t \in \{2, 3, 5\}$ and $n$ from $1$ to $500$, build trees by random insertion and check $2t^H - 1 \leq n \leq (2t)^{H+1} - 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The insertion maintains item 2 of @def-storage-engine, and the proposition holds for every tree satisfying it, so the check must pass; it tests
the implementation as much as the bound.

## Python

The check after each insertion.

```{.python .run}
import random
class Node:
    def __init__(self, keys=None, kids=None):
        self.keys, self.kids = keys or [], kids or []
def split(parent, i, t):
    full = parent.kids[i]
    right = Node(full.keys[t:], full.kids[t:])
    parent.keys.insert(i, full.keys[t - 1]); parent.kids.insert(i + 1, right)
    full.keys, full.kids = full.keys[:t - 1], full.kids[:t]
def insert(root, key, t):
    if len(root.keys) == 2 * t - 1:
        root = Node([], [root]); split(root, 0, t)
    node = root
    while node.kids:
        i = sum(k < key for k in node.keys)
        if len(node.kids[i].keys) == 2 * t - 1:
            split(node, i, t); i += key > node.keys[i]
        node = node.kids[i]
    node.keys.insert(sum(k < key for k in node.keys), key)
    return root
random.seed(10)
for t in (2, 3, 5):
    root, heights = Node(), set()
    for n, key in enumerate(random.sample(range(10**6), 500), 1):
        root = insert(root, key, t)
        H, node = 0, root
        while node.kids:
            node, H = node.kids[0], H + 1
        assert 2 * t**H - 1 <= n <= (2 * t)**(H + 1) - 1
        heights.add(H)
    print(f"t = {t}: bounds held for n = 1..500, heights seen {sorted(heights)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
t = 2: bounds held for n = 1..500, heights seen [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
t = 3: bounds held for n = 1..500, heights seen [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
t = 5: bounds held for n = 1..500, heights seen [0, 1, 2, 3]
```
::::
:::
::::

### The false-positive rate of a Bloom filter

A Bloom filter trades a small probability of a wrong "possibly" for memory: it stores no keys, only $m$ bits. How small depends on the bits per
key $m/n$ and on $k$. The analysis below follows Broder and Mitzenmacher and uses the
[Bernoulli](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-binomial-distribution) and
[independence](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-independence) rules of probability; we write $\zeta$
for the fraction of bits still $0$ after the $n$ insertions.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-bloom-false-positive}
#### False positives of a Bloom filter

Let a Bloom filter with $m$ bits and $k$ hash functions hold $n$ keys, where the $kn$ hash values of the keys and the $k$ hash values of a
queried $y \notin S$ are independent and uniform on $\{1, \dots, m\}$.

(a) Each bit is $0$ with probability $p' = (1 - 1/m)^{kn}$, and $p' \leq p = e^{-kn/m}$; so $\mathbb E\,\zeta = p'$.

(b) Given the filter, the probability that $y$ is a false positive is $(1 - \zeta)^k$; unconditionally it is
$\mathbb E(1 - \zeta)^k \geq (1 - p')^k$.

(c) As a function of real $k > 0$, the approximation $f(k) = (1 - e^{-kn/m})^k$ is minimised at $k = (m/n)\ln 2$, where $p = 1/2$ and
$f = 2^{-k} = (2^{-\ln 2})^{m/n} \approx 0.6185^{m/n}$.

(d) (Quoted from @broder2004network [Sec. 2.1, p. 489].) If $X = m\zeta$ is the number of $0$ bits, then for any $\varepsilon > 0$,
$\mathbb P(|X - p'm| \geq \varepsilon m) \leq 2e^{-2\varepsilon^2m^2/(nk)}$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) A fixed bit stays $0$ if none of the $kn$ independent hash values hits it; each misses it with probability $1 - 1/m$, so by
independence $\mathbb P(\text{bit is } 0) = (1 - 1/m)^{kn}$. Since $1 - x \leq e^{-x}$, $p' \leq e^{-kn/m}$. The expectation of $\zeta$, the
mean of the $m$ indicator variables of the bits being $0$, is $p'$ by linearity.

(b) Given the filter, the set of $1$ bits is fixed and has $(1 - \zeta)m$ elements. The $k$ hash values of $y$ are independent of the filter and
uniform, so each lands on a $1$ bit with probability $1 - \zeta$, and all $k$ do with probability $(1 - \zeta)^k$. Averaging over filters gives
$\mathbb E(1 - \zeta)^k$, and since $x \mapsto (1 - x)^k$ is convex on $[0, 1]$ for $k \geq 1$, Jensen's inequality gives
$\mathbb E(1 - \zeta)^k \geq (1 - \mathbb E\zeta)^k = (1 - p')^k$.

(c) Put $p = e^{-kn/m}$, which decreases from $1$ to $0$ as $k$ runs over $(0, \infty)$, so that $k = -(m/n)\ln p$ and
$$
\ln f = k\ln(1 - p) = -\frac{m}{n}\,\ln p\,\ln(1 - p).
$$
Minimising $f$ is maximising $\varphi(p) = \ln p\,\ln(1 - p)$ on $(0, 1)$. It is symmetric, $\varphi(p) = \varphi(1 - p)$, and
$$
\varphi'(p) = \frac{\ln(1 - p)}{p} - \frac{\ln p}{1 - p} = \frac{(1 - p)\ln(1 - p) - p\ln p}{p(1 - p)}.
$$
Let $\theta(x) = x\ln x - (1 - x)\ln(1 - x)$ on $(0, 1/2]$. Then $\theta(x) \to 0$ as $x \to 0$, $\theta(1/2) = 0$ and
$\theta''(x) = 1/x - 1/(1 - x) > 0$ on $(0, 1/2)$, so $\theta$ is strictly convex with zero limits at both ends and $\theta < 0$ inside. Hence
$\varphi'(p) = -\theta(p)/(p(1 - p)) > 0$ on $(0, 1/2)$: $\varphi$ increases up to $1/2$ and, by symmetry, decreases after it. Its maximum is at
$p = 1/2$, that is $e^{-kn/m} = 1/2$, $k = (m/n)\ln 2$, and there $f = (1/2)^k = 2^{-(m/n)\ln 2} = (e^{-(\ln 2)^2})^{m/n}$, with
$e^{-(\ln 2)^2} = 0.6185\ldots$ $\square$

Part (d) needs a martingale tail inequality, which Broder and Mitzenmacher cite rather than prove; it says that the fraction of zero bits is
within a small $\varepsilon$ of $p'$ except with exponentially small probability, so $(1 - \zeta)^k$, the rate of a given filter, is close to
$(1 - p')^k$ and, since $p'$ is within $O(1/m)$ of $p$ [@broder2004network, Sec. 2.1, p. 487], to the approximation $f$.
@fig-bf-false-positive compares $f$ at the optimal $k$ with simulated filters.

![False-positive rate of a Bloom filter against bits per key, at the best integer number of hash functions: the approximation
$(1 - e^{-kn/m})^k$ (line) and simulated filters (points).](figures/bloom_fp.svg){#fig-bf-false-positive width=65%}

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Sinha's ten-bit filter of @exm-se-sinha-bloom is tiny. The proposition rates it.

::: {#exm-bf-sinha}
#### Sinha's filter

With $m = 10$, $k = 2$ and $n = 3$, $p' = 0.9^6 = 0.531$ and $(1 - p')^2 = 0.220$: about one available username in five is reported taken.
The actual filter has $5$ zero bits, $\zeta = 0.5$, so its rate given the filter is $(1 - 0.5)^2 = 0.25$.

```{.python .run}
p1 = 0.9**6
print(f"p' = {p1:.3f}, (1 - p')^2 = {(1 - p1)**2:.3f}, given the filter {(1 - 0.5)**2:.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
p' = 0.531, (1 - p')^2 = 0.220, given the filter 0.25
```
:::

Ten bits per key is a common budget. Part (c) gives its best rate.

::: {#exm-bf-ten-bits}
#### Ten bits per key

With $m/n = 10$, the optimum is $k = 10\ln 2 = 6.93$, so $k = 7$, and $f = (1 - e^{-0.7})^7 = 0.0082$: under one false positive in a hundred
queries for $1.25$ bytes per key.

```{.python .run}
import math
print(f"k* = {10 * math.log(2):.2f}; f(7) = {(1 - math.exp(-0.7))**7:.4f}; 0.6185^10 = {0.6185**10:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
k* = 6.93; f(7) = 0.0082; 0.6185^10 = 0.0082
```
:::

The bound can be inverted to size a filter. One percent needs under ten bits per key.

::: {#exm-bf-one-percent}
#### Sizing for one percent

At the optimum $f = 2^{-(m/n)\ln 2}$, so $f = \varepsilon$ needs $m/n = -\ln\varepsilon/(\ln 2)^2$: $9.59$ bits per key for $1\%$ and $14.4$ for
$0.1\%$. For the $2 \times 10^7$ photos uploaded a day, a filter at $1\%$ takes $24\,\mathrm{MB}$.

```{.python .run}
import math
for eps in (0.01, 0.001):
    print(f"eps = {eps}: {-math.log(eps) / math.log(2)**2:.2f} bits per key")
print(f"one day of photos at 1%: {2e7 * -math.log(0.01) / math.log(2)**2 / 8 / 1e6:.0f} MB")
```

```{.text .run-output}
eps = 0.01: 9.59 bits per key
eps = 0.001: 14.38 bits per key
one day of photos at 1%: 24 MB
```
:::

The exact and approximate probabilities differ little. Part (a) bounds the difference's direction.

::: {#exm-bf-exact-vs-approx}
#### Exact against approximate

For $m = 1000$, $n = 100$, $k = 7$: $p' = 0.999^{700} = 0.49641$ and $p = e^{-0.7} = 0.49659$, so $p' \leq p$ as part (a) says, and the rates
$(1 - p')^7$ and $(1 - p)^7$ differ by under $0.5\%$.

```{.python .run}
import math
p1, p = 0.999**700, math.exp(-0.7)
print(f"p' = {p1:.5f}, p = {p:.5f}, (1-p')^7 = {(1 - p1)**7:.6f}, (1-p)^7 = {(1 - p)**7:.6f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
p' = 0.49641, p = 0.49659, (1-p')^7 = 0.008214, (1-p)^7 = 0.008194
```
:::

Part (b) rates a given filter from its bits. Counting zeros is enough.

::: {#exm-bf-given-filter}
#### Rating a given filter

A filter with $m = 10^5$ bits whose bit count shows $\zeta = 0.52$ has false-positive rate $(0.48)^k$ for every future query, by part (b): for
$k = 7$ that is $0.0059$, whatever keys produced it.
:::

Bigtable and Xu put a filter on each SSTable. Part (c) prices the reads saved.

::: {#exm-bf-sstables}
#### A filter per SSTable

With $10$ bits per key and $k = 7$ on each of $10$ SSTables, a lookup of a missing key reads $10 \times 0.0082 = 0.08$ SSTables on average, by
linearity of expectation, instead of $10$.
:::

The number of hash functions must be an integer. The loss from rounding is small.

::: {#exm-bf-integer-k}
#### Integer $k$

For $m/n = 8$, $k^* = 5.55$; $f(5) = 0.0217$ and $f(6) = 0.0216$, while the real optimum is $0.6185^8 = 0.0214$. Broder and Mitzenmacher note
that "a smaller, suboptimal k might be preferred since this reduces the number of hash functions" [@broder2004network, Sec. 2.1, p. 489].

```{.python .run}
import math
f = lambda k, r: (1 - math.exp(-k / r))**k
print(f"k* = {8 * math.log(2):.2f}; f(4) = {f(4, 8):.4f}, f(5) = {f(5, 8):.4f}, f(6) = {f(6, 8):.4f}, optimum {0.5**(8 * math.log(2)):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
k* = 5.55; f(4) = 0.0240, f(5) = 0.0217, f(6) = 0.0216, optimum 0.0214
```
:::

An optimal filter is half zeros. A filter can be checked by counting.

::: {#exm-bf-half-full}
#### Half full at the optimum

Part (c) says that the best filter has $p = 1/2$: half the bits set. A filter with many more ones than zeros holds more keys than it was sized for
and has a higher rate than planned, by part (b).
:::

Part (d) is a strong guarantee for large filters. The numbers show how strong.

::: {#exm-bf-concentration}
#### How concentrated?

For $m = 10^6$, $n = 10^5$, $k = 7$ and $\varepsilon = 0.01$, part (d) bounds the probability that the zero fraction is off by $0.01$ by
$2e^{-2 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 10^{12}/(7 \times 10^5)} = 2e^{-285.7}$, effectively zero.

```{.python .run}
import math
m, n, k, eps = 1e6, 1e5, 7, 0.01
print(f"exponent {-2 * eps**2 * m**2 / (n * k):.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
exponent -285.7
```
:::

A simulation shows the formula and the measured rate agreeing. It is the data of @fig-bf-false-positive at one point.

::: {#exm-bf-simulation}
#### A simulated filter

A filter with $m = 10^5$, $n = 10^4$, $k = 7$ built from random positions, queried with $10^5$ random non-members, has a measured rate close to
$(1 - \zeta)^7$ and to $f = 0.0082$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
m, n, k = 100_000, 10_000, 7
bits = np.zeros(m, bool); bits[rng.integers(0, m, n * k)] = True
zeta = 1 - bits.mean()
measured = bits[rng.integers(0, m, (100_000, k))].all(axis=1).mean()
print(f"zeta = {zeta:.4f}, (1 - zeta)^7 = {(1 - zeta)**7:.4f}, measured {measured:.4f}, f = {(1 - np.exp(-0.7))**7:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
zeta = 0.4969, (1 - zeta)^7 = 0.0082, measured 0.0086, f = 0.0082
```
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise sizes a filter for the photo service's usernames. It applies @exm-bf-one-percent.

::: {#exr-bf-usernames}
#### Usernames

The photo service checks username availability with a Bloom filter over $5 \times 10^8$ registered names and accepts a $0.1\%$ rate of "taken" for
free names. Find $m$, $k$ and the memory.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$m/n = -\ln 0.001/(\ln 2)^2 = 14.4$, so $m = 7.2 \times 10^9$ bits, $0.9\,\mathrm{GB}$, and $k = 14.4\ln 2 = 9.97$, so $k = 10$. A false positive
only sends the check to the database, so the filter never wrongly accepts a taken name, by @exr-se-no-false-negatives.

## Python

The parameters.

```{.python .run}
import math
n, eps = 5e8, 1e-3
r = -math.log(eps) / math.log(2)**2
print(f"bits per key {r:.1f}, m = {r * n:.2e} bits = {r * n / 8 / 1e9:.2f} GB, k = {r * math.log(2):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
bits per key 14.4, m = 7.19e+09 bits = 0.90 GB, k = 9.97
```
::::
:::

The second exercise checks the calculus behind part (c). Broder and Mitzenmacher give the derivative.

::: {#exr-bf-derivative}
#### The derivative

With $g(k) = k\ln(1 - e^{-kn/m})$, Broder and Mitzenmacher state $\partial g/\partial k = \ln(1 - e^{-kn/m}) + \frac{kn}{m}\frac{e^{-kn/m}}{1 -
e^{-kn/m}}$ [@broder2004network, Sec. 2.1, p. 489]. Verify the formula and that it vanishes at $k = (m/n)\ln 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By the product and chain rules, $g' = \ln(1 - e^{-kn/m}) + k \cdot \frac{(n/m)e^{-kn/m}}{1 - e^{-kn/m}}$, which is the formula. At
$e^{-kn/m} = 1/2$ it is $\ln\frac12 + \ln 2 \cdot \frac{1/2}{1/2} = 0$.

## Python

A finite-difference check.

```{.python .run}
import math
m, n = 1000, 100
g = lambda k: k * math.log(1 - math.exp(-k * n / m))
dg = lambda k: math.log(1 - math.exp(-k * n / m)) + k * n / m * math.exp(-k * n / m) / (1 - math.exp(-k * n / m))
k0, h = 5.0, 1e-6
print(f"formula {dg(k0):.6f}, finite difference {(g(k0 + h) - g(k0 - h)) / (2 * h):.6f}, at k* {dg(m / n * math.log(2)):.2e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
formula -0.162005, finite difference -0.162005, at k* 0.00e+00
```
::::
:::

The third exercise is the partitioned variant that Broder and Mitzenmacher discuss. Each hash function gets its own slice.

::: {#exr-bf-partitioned}
#### A partitioned filter

If each hash function has its own range of $m/k$ bits, a bit is $0$ with probability $(1 - k/m)^n$. Prove that $(1 - k/m)^n \leq (1 - 1/m)^{kn}$ for
$k \geq 1$, so the partitioned filter's zero fraction is smaller and its false-positive rate at least as large [@broder2004network, Sec. 2.1,
p. 488].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A bit in slice $i$ is hit only by $h_i$, once per key, with probability $k/m$; so it stays $0$ with probability $(1 - k/m)^n$. By Bernoulli's
inequality $(1 - 1/m)^k \geq 1 - k/m$ for $k \geq 1$ and $1/m \leq 1$, and raising both sides to the power $n$ gives the claim. Fewer zeros mean a
larger $(1 - \zeta)^k$.

## Python

Both probabilities for $m = 1000$, $n = 100$.

```{.python .run}
m, n = 1000, 100
for k in (1, 3, 7):
    print(f"k = {k}: partitioned {(1 - k / m)**n:.5f} <= shared {(1 - 1 / m)**(k * n):.5f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
k = 1: partitioned 0.90479 <= shared 0.90479
k = 3: partitioned 0.74048 <= shared 0.74071
k = 7: partitioned 0.49536 <= shared 0.49641
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise proves that filters with the same parameters can be merged. A bitwise OR is the filter of the union.

::: {#exr-bf-union}
#### Union by OR

Prove that the bitwise OR of the filters of $S_1$ and $S_2$, built with the same $m$ and hash functions, is the filter of $S_1 \cup S_2$, and use it
to merge the filters of two SSTables during compaction.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Bit $j$ of the filter of $S_1 \cup S_2$ is $1$ if and only if $h_i(x) = j$ for some $i$ and some $x \in S_1 \cup S_2$, that is, if and only if
it is $1$ in the filter of $S_1$ or in that of $S_2$. A compaction that keeps all keys of both inputs can OR their filters; one that drops keys
(tombstones, old versions) must rebuild, since bits cannot be cleared safely.

## Python

The two constructions agree.

```{.python .run}
import hashlib
m, k = 4096, 4
def filt(keys):
    b = 0
    for x in keys:
        for i in range(k):
            b |= 1 << (int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256(f"{i}:{x}".encode()).digest()[:4], "big") % m)
    return b
s1, s2 = {f"a{i}" for i in range(200)}, {f"b{i}" for i in range(150)}
print("OR equals filter of union:", filt(s1) | filt(s2) == filt(s1 | s2))
```

```{.text .run-output}
OR equals filter of union: True
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise shows that a Bloom filter cannot delete. Clearing a bit can create a false negative.

::: {#exr-bf-no-delete}
#### No deletion

Show with Sinha's filter of @exm-se-sinha-bloom that clearing the bits of "dave" to delete it makes the filter answer "not in $S$" for "john".
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

"dave" set bits $3$ and $5$, and "john" also uses bit $5$. Clearing both makes john's bit $5$ zero, so the filter reports john absent although he is
in $S$, contradicting @exr-se-no-false-negatives. In an LSM tree deletions are therefore tombstones, and filters are rebuilt when SSTables are.

## Python

The false negative.

```{.python .run}
bits = [0] * 10
names = {"john": (5, 8), "dave": (3, 5), "peter": (2, 9)}
for h in names.values():
    for p in h:
        bits[p] = 1
for p in names["dave"]:
    bits[p] = 0
print("john:", "possibly in S" if all(bits[p] for p in names["john"]) else "not in S (a false negative)")
```

```{.text .run-output}
john: not in S (a false negative)
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise shows what too many hash functions do. The rate has an interior minimum.

::: {#exr-bf-too-many-k}
#### Too many hash functions

For $m/n = 10$, tabulate $f(k)$ for $k = 1, \dots, 15$ and explain the shape with the two competing forces Broder and Mitzenmacher name: "using
more hash functions gives us more chances to find a 0 bit ... but using fewer hash functions increases the fraction of 0 bits"
[@broder2004network, Sec. 2.1, p. 488].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$f$ falls until $k = 7$ and rises after it: for small $k$, few probes of a mostly empty array; for large $k$, many probes of an array that is
mostly ones. Part (c) locates the minimum at $6.93$.

## Python

The table.

```{.python .run}
import math
print(" ".join(f"{k}:{(1 - math.exp(-k / 10))**k:.4f}" for k in range(1, 16)))
```

```{.text .run-output}
1:0.0952 2:0.0329 3:0.0174 4:0.0118 5:0.0094 6:0.0084 7:0.0082 8:0.0085 9:0.0091 10:0.0102 11:0.0116 12:0.0136 13:0.0160 14:0.0190 15:0.0227
```
::::

The seventh exercise checks part (b)'s inequality by simulation. Small filters make the gap visible.

::: {#exr-bf-jensen-gap}
#### The Jensen gap

For $m = 20$, $n = 4$, $k = 3$, estimate $\mathbb E(1 - \zeta)^k$ by simulating $10^5$ filters and compare with $(1 - p')^k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The mean of $(1 - \zeta)^3$ over filters exceeds $(1 - p')^3$, as Jensen's inequality says, because the zero fraction varies from filter to filter
when $m$ is small; part (d) says the gap vanishes as $m$ grows.

## Python

The simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
m, n, k, runs = 20, 4, 3, 100_000
hits = rng.integers(0, m, (runs, n * k))
ones = np.zeros((runs, m), bool); np.put_along_axis(ones, hits, True, axis=1)
zeta = 1 - ones.mean(axis=1)
p1 = (1 - 1 / m)**(n * k)
print(f"E(1-zeta)^k = {((1 - zeta)**k).mean():.4f} >= (1-p')^k = {(1 - p1)**k:.4f}; mean zeta {zeta.mean():.4f}, p' {p1:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
E(1-zeta)^k = 0.1018 >= (1-p')^k = 0.0971; mean zeta 0.5403, p' 0.5404
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise asks how many keys a sized filter can take. Overfilling degrades the rate quickly.

::: {#exr-bf-overfill}
#### Overfilling

A filter sized for $n_0$ keys at $1\%$ with the optimal $k = 7$ receives $2n_0$ keys. What is its rate?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$m/n_0 = 9.59$, so with $2n_0$ keys $m/n = 4.79$ and $f = (1 - e^{-7/4.79})^7 = 0.16$: sixteen times the planned rate. Part (c)'s optimum
assumes the planned $n$; filters on SSTables avoid the problem because an SSTable's keys are known when it is written.

## Python

The two rates.

```{.python .run}
import math
r = -math.log(0.01) / math.log(2)**2
for load in (1, 2):
    print(f"{load} x n0: f = {(1 - math.exp(-7 * load / r))**7:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 x n0: f = 0.0100
2 x n0: f = 0.1575
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise proves that $p'$ and $p$ are close. Broder and Mitzenmacher state it as "within $O(1/m)$".

::: {#exr-bf-p-close}
#### $p'$ is close to $p$

Prove that $0 \leq p - p' \leq p\,kn/m^2 \cdot(1 + O(1/m))$, and in particular $p - p' \leq e^{-1}/m \cdot (1 + O(1/m))$ when $kn = m$, using
$\ln(1 - x) \geq -x - x^2$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1/2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

With $x = 1/m$, $kn\ln(1 - x) \geq -kn/m - kn/m^2$, so $p' \geq p\,e^{-kn/m^2} \geq p(1 - kn/m^2)$ and $p - p' \leq p\,kn/m^2$; with $p'
\leq p$ from part (a), $0 \leq p - p' \leq p\,kn/m^2$. Writing $a = kn/m$, the bound is $a e^{-a}/m \leq e^{-1}/m$, since $ae^{-a}$ has maximum
$e^{-1}$ at $a = 1$: the difference is at most $0.37/m$ whatever $k$ and $n$ are, which is the $O(1/m)$ of the source.

## Python

The worst difference over $a$ for several $m$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
for m in (100, 10_000, 1_000_000):
    a = np.linspace(0.01, 10, 2000)
    diff = np.exp(-a) - (1 - 1 / m)**(a * m)
    print(f"m = {m:8d}: max (p - p') * m = {(diff * m).max():.4f} (bound e^-1 = {np.exp(-1):.4f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
m =      100: max (p - p') * m = 0.1847 (bound e^-1 = 0.3679)
m =    10000: max (p - p') * m = 0.1839 (bound e^-1 = 0.3679)
m =  1000000: max (p - p') * m = 0.1840 (bound e^-1 = 0.3679)
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise puts the filter in front of a database. The saving depends on the share of missing keys.

::: {#exr-bf-database-reads}
#### Reads saved

A service looks up $10^4$ keys per second, $70\%$ of which are absent, in a database that costs $5\,\mathrm{ms}$ of disk per lookup. With a filter
at $1\%$ in front, how much disk time per second is saved?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Present keys still go to the database ($3000$ lookups), absent keys go only on a false positive ($7000 \times 0.01 = 70$): $3070$ lookups instead of
$10^4$, saving $6930 \times 5\,\mathrm{ms} = 34.65$ disk-seconds per second, the work of about $35$ disks. This is Liu's use of a Bloom filter to
avoid expensive disk seeks [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 5, "Bloom Filter"].

## Python

The counts.

```{.python .run}
rate, absent, fp, cost = 1e4, 0.7, 0.01, 0.005
with_filter = rate * (1 - absent) + rate * absent * fp
print(f"lookups {with_filter:.0f} instead of {rate:.0f}; disk-seconds saved per second {(rate - with_filter) * cost:.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lookups 3070 instead of 10000; disk-seconds saved per second 34.65
```
::::
:::
::::

## Transactions and isolation {#sec-transactions}

When two requests change the same data at once, the result can be one that neither would produce alone. Liu's first example is a global
counter: two threads read $x = 1$, both add one, "each thread thinks x is now 2 and persists x as 2. Instead of 3, the final result becomes
2" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Concurrency Control and Transaction"]. A database avoids such outcomes by grouping operations
into transactions and controlling how concurrent transactions interleave. This section defines transactions, the anomalies that
interleaving causes and the isolation levels that exclude them, and proves that two-phase locking produces schedules equivalent to running
the transactions one at a time.

For more on this topic, see @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Concurrency Control and Transaction"], @sqliteIsolation,
@sqliteTransaction and @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 2.4.2].

### Transactions, anomalies and isolation levels

A transaction is the unit that the database makes atomic and isolates. Isolation is a matter of degree: the stronger levels exclude more
anomalies and allow less concurrency.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-transaction-isolation}
#### Transactions, schedules and isolation levels

1. A **transaction** is a sequence of reads $r(x)$ and writes $w(x)$ of data items by one client, ended by a **commit** or an **abort**. A
   database provides the **ACID** properties: **atomicity** (the writes of a transaction take effect all together or not at all),
   **consistency** (a transaction that preserves the integrity constraints when run alone leaves the database satisfying them),
   **isolation** (concurrent transactions affect each other only as the isolation level allows) and **durability** (the writes of a committed
   transaction survive crashes).
2. A **schedule** of transactions $T_1, \dots, T_k$ is an interleaving of their operations that keeps the order within each; it is **serial**
   if the transactions do not interleave. Two operations **conflict** if they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at
   least one is a write. Two schedules are **conflict-equivalent** if they contain the same operations and order every conflicting pair the
   same way, and a schedule is **conflict-serialisable** if it is conflict-equivalent to a serial schedule.
3. The **anomalies** of a schedule are: a **dirty read**, a read of a value written by a transaction that has not committed; a **lost
   update**, two transactions reading the same item and both writing it, so that the first write is overwritten without having been read by
   the second; a **non-repeatable read**, two reads of an item by one transaction that return different values because another transaction
   wrote it in between; **write skew**, two transactions reading overlapping data and writing different items, each keeping a constraint
   alone while together they break it; and a **phantom**, a query over a predicate whose result changes within a transaction because
   another inserts or deletes a matching row.
4. The **isolation levels** are, from weakest to strongest: **read uncommitted**, which allows dirty reads; **read committed**, which reads
   only committed values; **snapshot isolation**, in which each transaction reads the committed state as of its start and commits only if no
   transaction that committed since its start wrote an item it writes; and **serializable**, under which every schedule has the effect of a
   serial one.
5. Under **two-phase locking** (2PL) a transaction takes a shared lock on an item before reading it and an exclusive lock before writing it, a
   lock is not granted while another transaction holds a conflicting one (any lock conflicts with an exclusive lock), and no transaction
   acquires a lock after it has released one. Under **optimistic concurrency control** a transaction takes no locks; it records the version
   of each item it reads and, at commit, aborts if any of those versions has changed.
:::

::::

The names of the levels vary between databases, and a level is usually stated by the anomalies it rules out. SQLite, which runs the examples,
provides "serializable" isolation between connections, implemented "by actually serializing the writes"; in its write-ahead-log (WAL) mode
readers see a snapshot, and the only way to see uncommitted changes is a shared cache with `PRAGMA read_uncommitted`
[@sqliteIsolation].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Liu's counter is a lost update. Two SQLite connections reproduce it when each reads and then writes in a separate statement.

::: {#exm-tx-lost-counter}
#### Liu's counter

Each connection reads $x$, computes $x + 1$ and writes it back; with the reads interleaved, the second write overwrites the first.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3, tempfile, os
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "counter.db")
a, b = (sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None) for _ in range(2))
a.execute("CREATE TABLE counter(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, x INT)"); a.execute("INSERT INTO counter VALUES (1, 1)")
xa = a.execute("SELECT x FROM counter").fetchone()[0]
xb = b.execute("SELECT x FROM counter").fetchone()[0]
a.execute("UPDATE counter SET x = ? WHERE id = 1", (xa + 1,))
b.execute("UPDATE counter SET x = ? WHERE id = 1", (xb + 1,))
print("after two increments x =", a.execute("SELECT x FROM counter").fetchone()[0])
```

```{.text .run-output}
after two increments x = 2
```
:::

Atomicity is visible when a transaction fails halfway. Liu's file counter is the example.

::: {#exm-tx-atomic}
#### All or nothing

Liu's schema keeps a `number_of_files` per folder: "if the database increases number_of_files by 1 first and the operation to add a row to the
file table fails, number_of_files will get rolled back" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Relational Database"]. The run makes the
second statement violate a key and rolls back.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)
db.executescript("""CREATE TABLE folders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, number_of_files INT); INSERT INTO folders VALUES (1, 0);
                    CREATE TABLE files(name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, folder INT); INSERT INTO files VALUES ('a.txt', 1);""")
try:
    db.execute("BEGIN")
    db.execute("UPDATE folders SET number_of_files = number_of_files + 1 WHERE id = 1")
    db.execute("INSERT INTO files VALUES ('a.txt', 1)")           # duplicate name: fails
    db.execute("COMMIT")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    db.execute("ROLLBACK"); print("failed:", e)
print("number_of_files =", db.execute("SELECT number_of_files FROM folders").fetchone()[0])
```

```{.text .run-output}
failed: UNIQUE constraint failed: files.name
number_of_files = 0
```
:::

Liu's summary of ACID is informal. Item 1 sharpens it.

::: {#exm-tx-liu-acid}
#### Liu's ACID

Liu lists "Atomicity: The transaction is all-or-none", "Isolation: The transaction keeps other transactions from accessing or writing to the
same data until finished" and "Durability: Guarantees the data will not be lost" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Relational
Database"]. Isolation as described is the strongest form, achieved by locking; item 4 allows weaker ones, which is what most databases run
by default.
:::

Conflicts are pairs of operations. Listing them is mechanical.

::: {#exm-tx-conflicts}
#### Listing conflicts

In the schedule $r_1(x)\,r_2(x)\,w_1(x)\,w_2(x)$ of @exm-tx-lost-counter, the conflicting pairs are $(r_1(x), w_2(x))$, $(r_2(x), w_1(x))$ and
$(w_1(x), w_2(x))$; the two reads do not conflict.

```{.python .run}
s = [(1, "r", "x"), (2, "r", "x"), (1, "w", "x"), (2, "w", "x")]
pairs = [(a, b) for i, a in enumerate(s) for b in s[i + 1:] if a[0] != b[0] and a[2] == b[2] and "w" in (a[1], b[1])]
print([f"{a[1]}{a[0]}({a[2]}) < {b[1]}{b[0]}({b[2]})" for a, b in pairs])
```

```{.text .run-output}
['r1(x) < w2(x)', 'r2(x) < w1(x)', 'w1(x) < w2(x)']
```
:::

SQLite allows a dirty read only in one configuration. The run uses it.

::: {#exm-tx-dirty-read}
#### A dirty read

"The combined use of shared cache mode and the read_uncommitted pragma is the only way that one database connection can see uncommitted
changes on a different database connection" [@sqliteIsolation]. The reader sees a balance that is then rolled back.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
uri = "file:dirty?mode=memory&cache=shared"
w, r = (sqlite3.connect(uri, uri=True, isolation_level=None) for _ in range(2))
w.execute("CREATE TABLE acct(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, bal INT)"); w.execute("INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 100)")
w.execute("BEGIN"); w.execute("UPDATE acct SET bal = 0 WHERE id = 1")
r.execute("PRAGMA read_uncommitted = 1")
print("reader sees", r.execute("SELECT bal FROM acct").fetchone()[0], "before the writer's rollback")
w.execute("ROLLBACK")
print("committed value", r.execute("SELECT bal FROM acct").fetchone()[0])
```

```{.text .run-output}
reader sees 0 before the writer's rollback
committed value 100
```
:::

In WAL mode a SQLite reader keeps its snapshot. Changes committed after it started are invisible to it.

::: {#exm-tx-snapshot}
#### A snapshot

"When a read transaction starts, that reader continues to see an unchanging 'snapshot' of the database file as it existed at the moment in
time when the read transaction started" [@sqliteIsolation]. Reads within the transaction are repeatable.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3, tempfile, os
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "wal.db")
x, y = (sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None) for _ in range(2))
x.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")
x.execute("CREATE TABLE photos(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, likes INT)"); x.execute("INSERT INTO photos VALUES (1, 10)")
x.execute("BEGIN"); first = x.execute("SELECT likes FROM photos").fetchone()[0]
y.execute("UPDATE photos SET likes = 11 WHERE id = 1")
second = x.execute("SELECT likes FROM photos").fetchone()[0]; x.execute("COMMIT")
print(f"X reads {first} then {second} inside its transaction; after it, {x.execute('SELECT likes FROM photos').fetchone()[0]}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
X reads 10 then 10 inside its transaction; after it, 11
```
:::

A reader that later writes may find its snapshot out of date. SQLite then refuses the write.

::: {#exm-tx-busy-snapshot}
#### A stale snapshot cannot write

If X reads, Y commits an update, and X then tries to update, "the attempt by X to escalate its transaction from a read transaction to a write
transaction fails with an SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT error", since allowing it "would fork the history of the database file" [@sqliteIsolation].

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3, tempfile, os
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "wal.db")
x, y = (sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None, timeout=0) for _ in range(2))
x.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")
x.execute("CREATE TABLE photos(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, likes INT)"); x.execute("INSERT INTO photos VALUES (1, 10)")
x.execute("BEGIN"); x.execute("SELECT likes FROM photos").fetchone()
y.execute("UPDATE photos SET likes = 11 WHERE id = 1")
try:
    x.execute("UPDATE photos SET likes = 99 WHERE id = 1")
except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:
    print("X's write fails:", e.sqlite_errorname)
x.execute("ROLLBACK")
```

```{.text .run-output}
X's write fails: SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT
```
:::

Write skew needs two items and a constraint over both. Two doctors on call are the textbook case.

::: {#exm-tx-write-skew}
#### Write skew

At least one doctor must be on call. Two transactions each check that two doctors are on call and take a different doctor off; each alone is
correct, together they leave nobody. Liu's meeting rooms are the same anomaly: two threads check that a time range is free and both book it
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Write Skew With Phantom Data"]. Under snapshot isolation both commit, since they write different
rows; SQLite's serializable isolation rejects the second.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3, tempfile, os
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "oncall.db")
a, b = (sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None, timeout=0) for _ in range(2))
a.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")
a.execute("CREATE TABLE doctors(name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, on_call INT)"); a.execute("INSERT INTO doctors VALUES ('ana', 1), ('ben', 1)")
a.execute("BEGIN"); b.execute("BEGIN")
print("both see", a.execute("SELECT SUM(on_call) FROM doctors").fetchone()[0], "and", b.execute("SELECT SUM(on_call) FROM doctors").fetchone()[0], "on call")
a.execute("UPDATE doctors SET on_call = 0 WHERE name = 'ana'"); a.execute("COMMIT")
try:
    b.execute("UPDATE doctors SET on_call = 0 WHERE name = 'ben'"); b.execute("COMMIT")
except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:
    b.execute("ROLLBACK"); print("second transaction refused:", e.sqlite_errorname)
print("on call now:", a.execute("SELECT name FROM doctors WHERE on_call = 1").fetchall())
```

```{.text .run-output}
both see 2 and 2 on call
second transaction refused: SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT
on call now: [('ben',)]
```
:::

A phantom concerns rows that do not exist yet. Locking existing rows cannot prevent it.

::: {#exm-tx-phantom}
#### Phantoms and materialised slots

To book a room for 10:00-11:00, a transaction checks that no booking overlaps and inserts one; a concurrent transaction does the same. The
conflict is on a row that neither read, because it did not exist. Liu's remedies are to lock a superset (the room's row), a "predicate lock
based on queries", or to "materialize data": create a row per 30-minute block, so that booking becomes an update of existing rows
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Write Skew With Phantom Data"].
:::

Optimistic control checks a version at commit. Liu describes it with version numbers.

::: {#exm-tx-optimistic}
#### Version numbers

"When the second thread comes in with v1, when the database tries to commit, it checks that v1 is outdated against the current version number
v2 and fails the request" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Optimistic Locking"]. An update guarded by `WHERE version = ?` implements
the check in one statement.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE doc(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT, version INT)"); db.execute("INSERT INTO doc VALUES (1, 'draft', 1)")
def save(body, read_version):
    return db.execute("UPDATE doc SET body = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 1 AND version = ?", (body, read_version)).rowcount == 1
v = db.execute("SELECT version FROM doc").fetchone()[0]          # both editors read version 1
print("first save:", save("edit A", v), "| second save:", save("edit B", v), "|", db.execute("SELECT * FROM doc").fetchone())
```

```{.text .run-output}
first save: True | second save: False | (1, 'edit A', 2)
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise fixes Liu's counter. The increment must be one operation of the database.

::: {#exr-tx-counter-fix}
#### Fixing the counter

Eight clients, each with its own connection, increment a counter $500$ times in rounds in which every client reads before any client writes. Compare
the final value when each increment is a `SELECT` followed by an `UPDATE` with the final value when it is `UPDATE counter SET x = x + 1`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The single statement reads and writes under the database's write lock, so no increment is lost: $4000$. In the two-statement version all eight
clients read the same value in a round and write the same successor, so each round adds one: $500$, seven increments of eight lost.

## Python

Both versions, with the clients interleaved in rounds.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3, tempfile, os
def run(atomic):
    path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "c.db")
    clients = [sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None) for _ in range(8)]
    clients[0].execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL"); clients[0].execute("PRAGMA synchronous = OFF")
    clients[0].execute("CREATE TABLE counter(x INT)"); clients[0].execute("INSERT INTO counter VALUES (0)")
    for _ in range(500):
        if atomic:
            for c in clients:
                c.execute("UPDATE counter SET x = x + 1")
        else:
            seen = [c.execute("SELECT x FROM counter").fetchone()[0] for c in clients]
            for c, x in zip(clients, seen):
                c.execute("UPDATE counter SET x = ?", (x + 1,))
    return clients[0].execute("SELECT x FROM counter").fetchone()[0]
print("read then write:", run(False), "| single UPDATE:", run(True), "| expected 4000")
```

```{.text .run-output}
read then write: 500 | single UPDATE: 4000 | expected 4000
```
::::
:::

The second exercise analyses Tan's compare-and-set lock. One statement decides which editor wins.

::: {#exr-tx-tan-cas}
#### Tan's edit lock

Tan locks a configuration with `UPDATE ... SET unix_locked = {current time}, edit_username = ... WHERE unix_locked = {unix_locked}`, where
`{unix_locked}` is the value the client read [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 2.4.2, pp. 31-33]. Prove that of two clients that read the same
value, at most one acquires the lock, and simulate it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Each `UPDATE` is a transaction that reads and writes `unix_locked` atomically. Under serializable isolation the two run as if one after the
other; the first finds the value it read and changes it, so the second's condition fails and it updates no row. The client learns the outcome
from the number of rows updated. This is optimistic control with the timestamp as the version.

## Python

Two clients with the same read value.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE config(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, unix_locked INT, edit_username TEXT)"); db.execute("INSERT INTO config VALUES (1, 0, NULL)")
seen = db.execute("SELECT unix_locked FROM config").fetchone()[0]
for user, now in (("ana", 1700000000), ("ben", 1700000001)):
    got = db.execute("UPDATE config SET unix_locked = ?, edit_username = ? WHERE id = 1 AND unix_locked = ?", (now, user, seen)).rowcount
    print(user, "acquired the lock" if got else "did not acquire the lock")
```

```{.text .run-output}
ana acquired the lock
ben did not acquire the lock
```
::::
:::

The third exercise corrects Liu's description of consistency. It confuses two letters of ACID.

::: {#exr-tx-liu-consistency}
#### Atomicity or consistency?

Liu defines "Consistency: The transaction doesn't leave part of the data committed if the transaction fails" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020,
Ch. 5, "Relational Database"]. Which property of item 1 is this, and what does consistency mean instead? Give a constraint that SQLite enforces.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Not leaving part of a failed transaction committed is atomicity. Consistency is about integrity constraints: a transaction that preserves them
alone leaves them true. The database enforces declared constraints such as `CHECK (balance >= 0)`; other invariants are the application's
responsibility, and isolation guarantees that concurrent transactions do not break those that each preserves alone.

## Python

A `CHECK` constraint rejecting an overdraft.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE acct(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, balance INT CHECK (balance >= 0))"); db.execute("INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 50)")
try:
    db.execute("UPDATE acct SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE id = 1")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("rejected:", e)
```

```{.text .run-output}
rejected: CHECK constraint failed: balance >= 0
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise counts schedules. Serial ones are few among all interleavings.

::: {#exr-tx-count-schedules}
#### How many schedules?

Prove that $k$ transactions with $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k$ operations have $(\ell_1 + \dots + \ell_k)!/(\ell_1!\cdots\ell_k!)$ schedules, of which $k!$ are
serial, and evaluate for two transactions of three operations.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A schedule is determined by which positions each transaction occupies, since the order within each is fixed: the number of ways to split
$\sum\ell_i$ positions into labelled groups of sizes $\ell_i$ is the multinomial coefficient. A serial schedule is determined by the order of the
transactions, $k!$ choices. For two transactions of three operations: $20$ schedules, $2$ serial.

## Python

Enumeration for the small case.

```{.python .run}
from itertools import permutations
from math import factorial
ops = ["a1", "a2", "a3", "b1", "b2", "b3"]
valid = {p for p in permutations(ops) if [o for o in p if o[0] == "a"] == ops[:3] and [o for o in p if o[0] == "b"] == ops[3:]}
print(len(valid), "schedules;", factorial(6) // (factorial(3)**2), "by the formula")
```

```{.text .run-output}
20 schedules; 20 by the formula
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise names the anomaly in each of four schedules. The definitions of item 3 decide.

::: {#exr-tx-classify}
#### Naming anomalies

Name the anomaly: (i) $w_1(x)\,r_2(x)\,\text{abort}_1$; (ii) $r_1(x)\,w_2(x)\,\text{commit}_2\,r_1(x)$; (iii) $r_1(x)\,r_2(x)\,w_1(x)\,w_2(x)$; (iv)
$r_1(x)\,r_1(y)\,r_2(x)\,r_2(y)\,w_1(x)\,w_2(y)$ with the constraint $x + y \geq 1$ and both writes setting a value to $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(i) A dirty read: $T_2$ read a value that never committed. (ii) A non-repeatable read. (iii) A lost update. (iv) Write skew: each transaction
writes a different item after reading both.

## Python

The conflicts of (iv): they go both ways between the transactions.

```{.python .run}
s = [(1, "r", "x"), (1, "r", "y"), (2, "r", "x"), (2, "r", "y"), (1, "w", "x"), (2, "w", "y")]
edges = {(a[0], b[0]) for i, a in enumerate(s) for b in s[i + 1:] if a[0] != b[0] and a[2] == b[2] and "w" in (a[1], b[1])}
print("conflict edges of (iv):", sorted(edges))
```

```{.text .run-output}
conflict edges of (iv): [(1, 2), (2, 1)]
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise proves that snapshot isolation prevents non-repeatable reads and dirty reads. It follows from where reads come from.

::: {#exr-tx-si-reads}
#### What snapshots prevent

Prove from item 4 that snapshot isolation allows neither dirty reads nor non-repeatable reads.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Every read of $T$ (of an item $T$ has not written) returns the committed state at $T$'s start. A value written by an uncommitted transaction is not
part of any committed state, so it is never read: no dirty reads. Two reads of $x$ by $T$ both return $x$'s value in the same state, so they agree:
reads are repeatable. @exm-tx-snapshot shows it in SQLite.

## Python

A minimal snapshot store in which a reader sees its start state.

```{.python .run}
history = [{"x": 1}]                               # committed states
def begin():
    return len(history) - 1                       # snapshot index
def read(snap, k):
    return history[snap][k]
t = begin(); first = read(t, "x")
history.append({**history[-1], "x": 2})            # another transaction commits x = 2
print("T reads", first, "then", read(t, "x"), "| latest committed", history[-1]["x"])
```

```{.text .run-output}
T reads 1 then 1 | latest committed 2
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise proves that snapshot isolation prevents lost updates. The commit rule is what does it.

::: {#exr-tx-si-lost-update}
#### No lost updates under snapshots

Prove that under snapshot isolation two concurrent transactions that both write $x$ cannot both commit, so the lost update of @exm-tx-lost-counter
is impossible.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be concurrent, so each starts before the other commits, and suppose both write $x$. Whichever commits second, say $T_2$, finds
that $T_1$ committed after $T_2$'s start and wrote $x$, an item $T_2$ writes, so $T_2$ is not allowed to commit. The writer that is refused retries
from a new snapshot, in which it reads the committed increment.

## Python

The commit rule on the counter.

```{.python .run}
committed, log = {"x": 1}, []                       # log: (commit time, items written)
clock = 0
def start():
    return {"t": clock, "reads": dict(committed), "writes": {}}
def commit(tx):
    global clock
    if any(t > tx["t"] and set(items) & set(tx["writes"]) for t, items in log):
        return False
    clock += 1; log.append((clock, list(tx["writes"]))); committed.update(tx["writes"]); return True
a, b = start(), start()
a["writes"]["x"] = a["reads"]["x"] + 1; b["writes"]["x"] = b["reads"]["x"] + 1
print("A commits:", commit(a), "| B commits:", commit(b), "| x =", committed["x"])
```

```{.text .run-output}
A commits: True | B commits: False | x = 2
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise shows that snapshot isolation allows write skew. The same commit rule lets both doctors leave.

::: {#exr-tx-si-write-skew}
#### Write skew under snapshots

Using the store of @exr-tx-si-lost-update, run the two doctors of @exm-tx-write-skew under snapshot isolation and explain why both commit.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The transactions write different items, `ana` and `ben`, so the commit rule finds no common written item and accepts both; the constraint, which
depends on both items, is broken. Snapshot isolation is therefore weaker than serializable, and SQLite's refusal in @exm-tx-write-skew comes from
its single writer, not from the snapshot.

## Python

Both commits succeed.

```{.python .run}
committed, log, clock = {"ana": 1, "ben": 1}, [], 0
def start():
    return {"t": clock, "reads": dict(committed), "writes": {}}
def commit(tx):
    global clock
    if any(t > tx["t"] and set(items) & set(tx["writes"]) for t, items in log):
        return False
    clock += 1; log.append((clock, list(tx["writes"]))); committed.update(tx["writes"]); return True
a, b = start(), start()
if sum(a["reads"].values()) >= 2: a["writes"]["ana"] = 0
if sum(b["reads"].values()) >= 2: b["writes"]["ben"] = 0
print("A commits:", commit(a), "| B commits:", commit(b), "| on call:", sum(committed.values()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
A commits: True | B commits: True | on call: 0
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise uses SQLite's advice for transactions that will write. Starting as a writer avoids the stale snapshot.

::: {#exr-tx-begin-immediate}
#### `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`

The SQLite documentation advises that a transaction that "will eventually want to write" can "issue BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... If the BEGIN IMMEDIATE
operation succeeds, then no subsequent operations in that transaction will ever fail with an SQLITE_BUSY error" [@sqliteIsolation]. Redo
@exm-tx-busy-snapshot with X starting `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, and say what happens to Y.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

X takes the write lock at once; Y's update now fails with `SQLITE_BUSY` (it would wait with a timeout), and X's update succeeds. The conflict is
resolved at the start, before X has done work it would have to discard.

## Python

The reordered failure.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3, tempfile, os
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "wal.db")
x, y = (sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None, timeout=0) for _ in range(2))
x.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")
x.execute("CREATE TABLE photos(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, likes INT)"); x.execute("INSERT INTO photos VALUES (1, 10)")
x.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE"); x.execute("SELECT likes FROM photos").fetchone()
try:
    y.execute("UPDATE photos SET likes = 11 WHERE id = 1")
except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:
    print("Y's write fails:", e.sqlite_errorname)
x.execute("UPDATE photos SET likes = 99 WHERE id = 1"); x.execute("COMMIT")
print("likes =", y.execute("SELECT likes FROM photos").fetchone()[0])
```

```{.text .run-output}
Y's write fails: SQLITE_BUSY
likes = 99
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise prices optimistic control under contention. The number of attempts is geometric.

::: {#exr-tx-optimistic-retries}
#### Retries under contention

If each attempt of an optimistic transaction fails independently with probability $q$, prove that the number of attempts is
[geometric](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-binomial-distribution) with mean $1/(1 - q)$, and simulate
$q = 0.5$. Liu warns that with many writers "it can lead to many failures and retries" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Optimistic
Locking"].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The attempts are independent trials that succeed with probability $1 - q$, and the number of attempts until the first success is geometric with
parameter $1 - q$, of mean $1/(1 - q)$: $2$ attempts for $q = 0.5$, $10$ for $q = 0.9$. Under high contention, waiting for a lock wastes less work
than repeating the transaction.

## Python

A simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
for q in (0.5, 0.9):
    print(f"q = {q}: mean attempts {rng.geometric(1 - q, 100_000).mean():.3f}, formula {1 / (1 - q):.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
q = 0.5: mean attempts 1.997, formula 2.0
q = 0.9: mean attempts 9.988, formula 10.0
```
::::
:::
::::

### Serialisability and two-phase locking

Serializable isolation asks that a schedule have the effect of some serial one. Conflict-serialisability is a condition that can be checked
on the schedule itself, through a graph, and two-phase locking guarantees it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-serializability}
#### Precedence graphs and two-phase locking

The **precedence graph** of a schedule has a vertex for each transaction and an edge $T_i \to T_j$ whenever an operation of $T_i$ precedes and
conflicts with an operation of $T_j$.

(a) A schedule is conflict-serialisable if and only if its precedence graph has no cycle, and its conflict-equivalent serial schedules are those
that order the transactions by a topological order of the graph.

(b) Every schedule in which all transactions follow two-phase locking is conflict-serialisable: ordering the transactions by the time at which each
acquires its last lock gives an equivalent serial schedule.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) Suppose the schedule $s$ is conflict-equivalent to a serial schedule $s'$. An edge $T_i \to T_j$ comes from a conflicting pair with the
operation of $T_i$ first in $s$, hence first in $s'$, so $T_i$ precedes $T_j$ in $s'$. All edges therefore go forward in the order of $s'$, which
is a topological order, and a graph with a topological order has no cycle. Conversely, suppose the graph has no cycle, so it has a topological
order, and let $s'$ run the transactions serially in that order. $s'$ has the operations of $s$, with the order within each transaction kept. If
$o_i$ of $T_i$ precedes a conflicting $o_j$ of $T_j$ in $s$, then $T_i \to T_j$ is an edge, so $T_i$ comes before $T_j$ in $s'$ and $o_i$ precedes
$o_j$ in $s'$. So $s$ and $s'$ order every conflicting pair alike. The first part also shows that every equivalent serial schedule follows a
topological order.

(b) Let $\sigma_i$ be the time at which $T_i$ acquires its last lock, its **lock point**. Take an edge $T_i \to T_j$, from $o_i$ of $T_i$ on item $x$
preceding a conflicting $o_j$ of $T_j$ on $x$. At least one of them is a write, so the lock $T_i$ holds on $x$ at $o_i$ and the lock $T_j$ holds on
$x$ at $o_j$ conflict and are never held at the same time: the interval during which $T_i$ holds its lock ends before the interval of $T_j$'s
begins, because it contains the time of $o_i$, which is earlier than that of $o_j$. Hence $T_i$ releases a lock before $T_j$ acquires one, and by the
two-phase rule $T_i$ acquired all its locks before its first release:
$$
\sigma_i \;<\; \text{release}_i(x) \;\leq\; \text{acquire}_j(x) \;\leq\; \sigma_j.
$$
Every edge goes from a smaller lock point to a larger one, so ordering by lock points is a topological order; by (a) the schedule is conflict-
serialisable, and that order gives an equivalent serial schedule. $\square$

The theorem concerns operations on existing items. A phantom of @exm-tx-phantom involves a row that no transaction locked, which is why Liu's
remedies lock a predicate, a superset or materialised rows. 2PL can also deadlock, two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds; the
database then aborts one, and the theorem applies to the transactions that remain.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The lost update has a cycle. No serial order explains it.

::: {#exm-ser-lost-update-cycle}
#### The lost update is not serialisable

In $r_1(x)\,r_2(x)\,w_1(x)\,w_2(x)$ the pair $(r_1(x), w_2(x))$ gives $T_1 \to T_2$ and $(r_2(x), w_1(x))$ gives $T_2 \to T_1$: a cycle, so by part
(a) the schedule is not conflict-serialisable.

```{.python .run}
def graph(s):
    return {(a[0], b[0]) for i, a in enumerate(s) for b in s[i + 1:] if a[0] != b[0] and a[2] == b[2] and "w" in (a[1], b[1])}
print(sorted(graph([(1, "r", "x"), (2, "r", "x"), (1, "w", "x"), (2, "w", "x")])))
```

```{.text .run-output}
[(1, 2), (2, 1)]
```
:::

Interleaving does not by itself break serialisability. Here is a schedule that is equivalent to a serial one.

::: {#exm-ser-interleaved-ok}
#### An interleaved serialisable schedule

$r_1(x)\,w_1(x)\,r_2(x)\,r_1(y)\,w_2(x)\,w_1(y)$ has the edges $T_1 \to T_2$ only (on $x$), so it is equivalent to the serial schedule $T_1T_2$:
$T_2$ touches only $x$, after $T_1$ has finished with it.
:::

The test of part (a) is a topological sort. Python's standard library has one.

::: {#exm-ser-checker}
#### A serialisability checker

The run builds the precedence graph and asks `graphlib` for a topological order, which fails exactly when there is a cycle.

