```{.python .run}
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter, CycleError
def serial_order(s):
    ts = TopologicalSorter({t: set() for t, _, _ in s})
    for i, a in enumerate(s):
        for b in s[i + 1:]:
            if a[0] != b[0] and a[2] == b[2] and "w" in (a[1], b[1]):
                ts.add(b[0], a[0])
    try:
        return list(ts.static_order())
    except CycleError:
        return None
ok = [(1, "r", "x"), (1, "w", "x"), (2, "r", "x"), (1, "r", "y"), (2, "w", "x"), (1, "w", "y")]
bad = [(1, "r", "x"), (2, "r", "x"), (1, "w", "x"), (2, "w", "x")]
print("interleaved:", serial_order(ok), "| lost update:", serial_order(bad))
```

```{.text .run-output}
interleaved: [1, 2] | lost update: None
```
:::

Under 2PL the lost update cannot happen. The two transactions deadlock instead.

::: {#exm-ser-2pl-deadlock}
#### 2PL turns the lost update into a deadlock

Both transactions take shared locks on $x$ to read it. To write, $T_1$ needs an exclusive lock, which waits for $T_2$'s shared lock, and $T_2$ needs
one too, which waits for $T_1$'s: each waits for the other. The database aborts one, say $T_2$, and $T_1$ completes; $T_2$ retries and reads the new
value.
:::

A schedule produced by 2PL shows its lock points. The serial order of part (b) follows them.

::: {#exm-ser-lock-points}
#### Lock points

In $\ell_1(x)\,r_1(x)\,w_1(x)\,\ell_1(y)\,u_1(x)\,\ell_2(x)\,r_2(x)\,w_2(x)\,u_2(x)\,r_1(y)\,w_1(y)\,u_1(y)$, where $\ell$ acquires and $u$ releases
an exclusive lock, $T_1$'s lock point is $\ell_1(y)$ and $T_2$'s is $\ell_2(x)$. $T_1$'s comes first, and the schedule is equivalent to $T_1T_2$,
although $T_1$ finishes last.
:::

Holding all locks until commit is the common variant. It also prevents dirty reads.

::: {#exm-ser-strict}
#### Strict two-phase locking

If every transaction holds its exclusive locks until it commits or aborts, no other transaction can read an item it wrote before it commits: dirty
reads, and the cascading aborts they would cause, are impossible, and part (b) still applies since releasing at the end is a special case of two
phases.
:::

Write skew also has a cycle. The edges come from reads and writes of different items.

::: {#exm-ser-write-skew-cycle}
#### Write skew has a cycle

In the schedule of @exr-tx-classify (iv), $r_2(x)$ precedes $w_1(x)$, giving $T_2 \to T_1$, and $r_1(y)$ precedes $w_2(y)$, giving $T_1 \to T_2$: a
cycle, so no serial order explains it, although no item was written twice.
:::

SQLite serialises writers with one lock on the database. That is two-phase locking at the coarsest scope.

::: {#exm-ser-sqlite-database-lock}
#### One lock for the database

"There can only be a single writer at a time to an SQLite database" [@sqliteIsolation]: writers hold an exclusive lock on the whole database until
they commit, Liu's "Database Lock" scope with its "extremely low throughput" for writes [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Scope of the Lock"].
The equivalent serial order of writers is their commit order.
:::

A graph without edges allows every order. Transactions on disjoint items are the case.

::: {#exm-ser-no-edges}
#### Disjoint transactions

If $k$ transactions touch disjoint items, the graph has no edges and each of the $k!$ serial orders is equivalent to the schedule, by part (a). Row-level
locking exploits this: transactions on different rows never wait.
:::

A ticket booking turns a phantom into a conflict. Materialising the seats is the trick.

::: {#exm-ser-seats}
#### Seats as rows

If each seat is a row with a `booked_by` column, two bookings of seat 12 both write the row, a conflict on an existing item, and 2PL or the commit rule
of snapshot isolation orders them; Liu's ticket booking system is exactly this case [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Design a Ticket Booking
System"].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise applies the checker of @exm-ser-checker. Three schedules over three transactions are tested.

::: {#exr-ser-three}
#### Three schedules

Decide which are conflict-serialisable and give a serial order: (i) $r_1(x)\,w_2(x)\,r_3(x)\,w_1(y)\,r_2(y)$; (ii) $r_1(x)\,w_2(x)\,w_3(y)\,r_1(y)$;
(iii) $w_1(x)\,r_2(x)\,w_2(y)\,r_3(y)\,w_3(x)\,r_1(z)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(i) Edges $T_1 \to T_2$ and $T_2 \to T_3$ on $x$ (the reads $r_1(x)$ and $r_3(x)$ do not conflict) and $T_1 \to T_2$ on $y$: acyclic, order
$T_1T_2T_3$. (ii) $T_1 \to T_2$ on $x$ and
$T_3 \to T_1$ on $y$: order $T_3T_1T_2$. (iii) $T_1 \to T_2$, $T_2 \to T_3$, $T_1 \to T_3$ and $T_2 \to T_3$ again: order $T_1T_2T_3$; $r_1(z)$ conflicts
with nothing.

## Python

The checker on the three schedules.

```{.python .run}
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter, CycleError
def serial_order(s):
    ts = TopologicalSorter({t: set() for t, _, _ in s})
    for i, a in enumerate(s):
        for b in s[i + 1:]:
            if a[0] != b[0] and a[2] == b[2] and "w" in (a[1], b[1]):
                ts.add(b[0], a[0])
    try:
        return list(ts.static_order())
    except CycleError:
        return None
for s in ([(1, "r", "x"), (2, "w", "x"), (3, "r", "x"), (1, "w", "y"), (2, "r", "y")],
          [(1, "r", "x"), (2, "w", "x"), (3, "w", "y"), (1, "r", "y")],
          [(1, "w", "x"), (2, "r", "x"), (2, "w", "y"), (3, "r", "y"), (3, "w", "x"), (1, "r", "z")]):
    print(serial_order(s))
```

```{.text .run-output}
[1, 2, 3]
[3, 1, 2]
[1, 2, 3]
```
::::
:::

The second exercise shows that 2PL is sufficient but not necessary. Some serialisable schedules break the two-phase rule.

::: {#exr-ser-2pl-not-necessary}
#### Serialisable but not two-phase

Prove that $r_1(x)\,w_2(x)\,r_1(y)$ is conflict-serialisable but cannot be produced when both transactions follow 2PL.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The only conflict is $r_1(x)$ before $w_2(x)$, so the graph has the single edge $T_1 \to T_2$ and the schedule is equivalent to $T_1T_2$. Under 2PL,
$T_2$ needs an exclusive lock on $x$ for $w_2(x)$, so $T_1$ must have released its shared lock on $x$ before then; but $T_1$ still has to lock $y$ for
$r_1(y)$, after that release, which the two-phase rule forbids.

## Python

The precedence graph.

```{.python .run}
s = [(1, "r", "x"), (2, "w", "x"), (1, "r", "y")]
print({(a[0], b[0]) for i, a in enumerate(s) for b in s[i + 1:] if a[0] != b[0] and a[2] == b[2] and "w" in (a[1], b[1])})
```

```{.text .run-output}
{(1, 2)}
```
::::
:::

The third exercise counts the equivalent serial orders. They are the topological orders.

::: {#exr-ser-count-orders}
#### How many serial orders?

Four transactions have the precedence edges $T_1 \to T_3$ and $T_2 \to T_3$ only. How many serial schedules are conflict-equivalent to the schedule?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (a), the topological orders: $T_3$ after $T_1$ and $T_2$, $T_4$ anywhere. Of the $24$ orders, those with $T_3$ last among $T_1, T_2, T_3$ are a
third, $8$.

## Python

Enumeration.

```{.python .run}
from itertools import permutations
edges = [(1, 3), (2, 3)]
print(sum(all(p.index(a) < p.index(b) for a, b in edges) for p in permutations([1, 2, 3, 4])))
```

```{.text .run-output}
8
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise simulates a lock manager. Every committed schedule must pass the test of part (a).

::: {#exr-ser-simulate-2pl}
#### Simulating strict 2PL

Generate random transactions of four operations over three items, interleave them at random under strict 2PL (a blocked transaction waits; on a
deadlock the youngest transaction is aborted and its operations removed), and check that the committed schedule is conflict-serialisable in $500$ runs.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (b) says every run passes. The simulation grants a lock when no other transaction holds a conflicting one, releases all of a transaction's locks
when it commits, and resolves each deadlock by aborting the transaction with the largest index.

## Python

The lock manager and the check.

```{.python .run}
import random
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter, CycleError
def acyclic(s):
    ts = TopologicalSorter({t: set() for t, _, _ in s})
    for i, a in enumerate(s):
        for b in s[i + 1:]:
            if a[0] != b[0] and a[2] == b[2] and "w" in (a[1], b[1]):
                ts.add(b[0], a[0])
    try:
        list(ts.static_order()); return True
    except CycleError:
        return False
random.seed(14)
passed, aborts = 0, 0
for run in range(500):
    txs = {t: [(random.choice("rw"), random.choice("xyz")) for _ in range(4)] for t in range(3)}
    pos, locks, done, schedule = {t: 0 for t in txs}, {}, set(), []          # locks: item -> {tx: mode}
    while len(done) < len(txs):
        ready = []
        for t in txs:
            if t in done:
                continue
            op, item = txs[t][pos[t]]
            held = locks.get(item, {})
            if all(o == t or (op == "r" and m == "r") for o, m in held.items()):
                ready.append(t)
        if not ready:                                                       # deadlock: abort the youngest active
            victim = max(t for t in txs if t not in done)
            schedule = [e for e in schedule if e[0] != victim]
            for h in locks.values():
                h.pop(victim, None)
            done.add(victim); aborts += 1; continue
        t = random.choice(ready); op, item = txs[t][pos[t]]
        h = locks.setdefault(item, {}); h[t] = "w" if op == "w" or h.get(t) == "w" else "r"
        schedule.append((t, op, item)); pos[t] += 1
        if pos[t] == 4:
            done.add(t)
            for h in locks.values():
                h.pop(t, None)
    passed += acyclic(schedule)
print(f"serialisable committed schedules: {passed}/500 (deadlock aborts: {aborts})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
serialisable committed schedules: 500/500 (deadlock aborts: 322)
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise proves that strict 2PL prevents dirty reads. It is the claim of @exm-ser-strict.

::: {#exr-ser-strict-no-dirty}
#### No dirty reads under strict 2PL

Prove that if every transaction holds its exclusive locks until it commits or aborts, no transaction reads a value written by an uncommitted transaction.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Suppose $T_j$ reads $x$ after $T_i$ wrote it. $T_i$ held an exclusive lock on $x$ from before the write until its commit or abort; $T_j$ needs a shared
lock on $x$, which conflicts and is granted only after $T_i$ releases, that is after $T_i$ committed or aborted. If $T_i$ aborted, its write was undone
before the release, so $T_j$ reads a committed value in either case.

## Python

The lock table refuses the reader while the writer is active.

```{.python .run}
locks = {"x": {"T1": "w"}}                         # T1 wrote x and has not committed
def can_read(t, item):
    return all(o == t or m == "r" for o, m in locks.get(item, {}).items())
print("T2 may read x before T1 commits:", can_read("T2", "x"))
locks["x"].pop("T1")                               # T1 commits and releases
print("after T1 commits:", can_read("T2", "x"))
```

```{.text .run-output}
T2 may read x before T1 commits: False
after T1 commits: True
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise counts the serialisable interleavings of two read-modify-write transactions. Only the serial ones are.

::: {#exr-ser-random-fraction}
#### Interleavings of two increments

For two transactions that each read $x$ and then write $x$, prove that exactly the $2$ serial schedules out of $6$ are conflict-serialisable.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

There are $\binom42 = 6$ schedules. In a non-serial one the second operation belongs to the other transaction; since each transaction reads before it
writes, the first two operations are then both reads, and both writes follow. So $r_1(x)$ precedes $w_2(x)$ and $r_2(x)$ precedes $w_1(x)$, giving
edges both ways: a cycle. The two serial schedules have edges in one direction only.

## Python

All six, tested.

```{.python .run}
from itertools import combinations
for slots in combinations(range(4), 2):
    s, it1, it2 = [], iter([(1, "r", "x"), (1, "w", "x")]), iter([(2, "r", "x"), (2, "w", "x")])
    s = [next(it1) if i in slots else next(it2) for i in range(4)]
    e = {(a[0], b[0]) for i, a in enumerate(s) for b in s[i + 1:] if a[0] != b[0] and a[2] == b[2] and "w" in (a[1], b[1])}
    print(" ".join(f"{o}{t}" for t, o, _ in s), "serialisable" if len(e) < 2 else "cycle")
```

```{.text .run-output}
r1 w1 r2 w2 serialisable
r1 r2 w1 w2 cycle
r1 r2 w2 w1 cycle
r2 r1 w1 w2 cycle
r2 r1 w2 w1 cycle
r2 w2 r1 w1 serialisable
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise extracts the lock-point order. It is the order of part (b).

::: {#exr-ser-lock-point-order}
#### Ordering by lock points

For the 2PL schedule of @exm-ser-lock-points, compute each transaction's lock point from the list of events and check that the lock-point order is a
topological order of the precedence graph.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$T_1$'s last acquisition is event $4$, $T_2$'s event $6$, so the order is $T_1T_2$; the only edge is $T_1 \to T_2$ on $x$, which the order respects.

## Python

The events and the check.

```{.python .run}
ev = [("l", 1, "x"), ("r", 1, "x"), ("w", 1, "x"), ("l", 1, "y"), ("u", 1, "x"), ("l", 2, "x"), ("r", 2, "x"), ("w", 2, "x"),
      ("u", 2, "x"), ("r", 1, "y"), ("w", 1, "y"), ("u", 1, "y")]
lp = {t: max(i for i, (k, tt, _) in enumerate(ev, 1) if k == "l" and tt == t) for t in (1, 2)}
ops = [(t, k, x) for k, t, x in ev if k in "rw"]
edges = {(a[0], b[0]) for i, a in enumerate(ops) for b in ops[i + 1:] if a[0] != b[0] and a[2] == b[2] and "w" in (a[1], b[1])}
print("lock points", lp, "| edges", edges, "| respected:", all(lp[a] < lp[b] for a, b in edges))
```

```{.text .run-output}
lock points {1: 4, 2: 6} | edges {(1, 2)} | respected: True
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise detects deadlocks with a graph. A cycle of waiting is the criterion.

::: {#exr-ser-wait-for}
#### The wait-for graph

Draw an edge $T_i \to T_j$ when $T_i$ waits for a lock held by $T_j$. Prove that the transactions are deadlocked if and only if this graph has a cycle,
when every transaction waits for at most one lock at a time and holders that are not waiting eventually proceed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If there is a cycle, each transaction on it waits for the next, which waits too, so none of them can proceed: a deadlock. If there is no cycle, follow
the edges from a waiting transaction; since the graph is finite and acyclic, the path ends at a transaction that does not wait, which proceeds and
eventually commits or aborts, releasing its locks; by induction on the length of the longest path, every waiting transaction is eventually granted
its lock. In @exm-ser-2pl-deadlock the graph is $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_1$.

## Python

The cycle test on the example.

```{.python .run}
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter, CycleError
waits = {"T1": {"T2"}, "T2": {"T1"}}
try:
    list(TopologicalSorter(waits).static_order()); print("no deadlock")
except CycleError as e:
    print("deadlock, cycle:", e.args[1])
```

```{.text .run-output}
deadlock, cycle: ['T1', 'T2', 'T1']
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise prevents a double booking with a constraint. The database turns the phantom into a conflict.

::: {#exr-ser-unique-booking}
#### A unique slot

Store bookings as `(room, slot)` with a `UNIQUE` constraint, where slots are Liu's $30$-minute blocks, and show that the second of two bookings for the
same slot fails while a booking of another slot succeeds.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The unique index makes the two inserts conflict on its key: whichever transaction inserts second finds the key present and fails. The predicate
"no overlapping booking" becomes the existence of a row, which the database can lock and check.

## Python

The two bookings and a third.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE bookings(room INT, slot INT, who TEXT, UNIQUE (room, slot))")
for who, slot in (("ana", 20), ("ben", 20), ("cai", 21)):
    try:
        db.execute("INSERT INTO bookings VALUES (1, ?, ?)", (slot, who)); print(who, "booked slot", slot)
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
        print(who, "refused: slot", slot, "taken")
```

```{.text .run-output}
ana booked slot 20
ben refused: slot 20 taken
cai booked slot 21
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise proves the easy direction of part (a) on serial schedules. It shows that serial schedules pass the test.

::: {#exr-ser-serial-acyclic}
#### Serial schedules pass

Prove directly that the precedence graph of a serial schedule has no cycle, and that a schedule with a cycle of length two contains two conflicting pairs
ordered in opposite ways.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

In a serial schedule all operations of $T_i$ precede those of $T_j$ when $T_i$ runs first, so every edge goes from an earlier to a later transaction
and a cycle would return to an earlier one, which is impossible. A cycle $T_i \to T_j \to T_i$ consists of a conflicting pair with $T_i$'s operation
first and another with $T_j$'s first; no serial schedule orders both pairs as the schedule does.

## Python

Every serial schedule of three random transactions has an acyclic graph.

```{.python .run}
import random
from itertools import permutations
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter, CycleError
random.seed(15)
txs = {t: [(t, random.choice("rw"), random.choice("xy")) for _ in range(3)] for t in (1, 2, 3)}
ok = True
for order in permutations(txs):
    s = [op for t in order for op in txs[t]]
    ts = TopologicalSorter({t: set() for t in txs})
    for i, a in enumerate(s):
        for b in s[i + 1:]:
            if a[0] != b[0] and a[2] == b[2] and "w" in (a[1], b[1]):
                ts.add(b[0], a[0])
    try:
        list(ts.static_order())
    except CycleError:
        ok = False
print("all 6 serial schedules acyclic:", ok)
```

```{.text .run-output}
all 6 serial schedules acyclic: True
```
::::
:::
::::

## File, block and object storage {#sec-storage-services}

Beneath every database lies a storage service, and the photo service's photos, which are too large for its database, go to one directly. Reis and
Housley distinguish three abstractions: files in a directory tree, raw blocks addressed by number, and immutable objects addressed by key
[@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 6, pp. 199-208]. When the data outgrows one machine, a distributed file system spreads files over
many; the Google File System, whose design starts from the observation that "component failures are the norm rather than the exception"
[@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 1], is the classic design and the model of HDFS. This section defines the three kinds of storage and the distributed
file system.

For more on this topic, see @reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022 [Ch. 6, "File Storage", "Block Storage" and "Object Storage"],
@ghemawat2003google [Secs. 2 and 3], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 4.3.5] and @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Cold Storage"].

### Block, file and object storage and distributed file systems

The three kinds differ in what they name and what they let a client change. Block storage names fixed-size blocks and lets any of them be rewritten;
file storage names files in a tree and lets bytes be appended or rewritten; object storage names whole objects and lets them only be replaced.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-storage-kinds}
#### Block, file and object storage and the distributed file system

1. **Block storage** presents a device as an array of fixed-size **blocks**, typically of $4096\,\mathrm{B}$, each read or written by its number. It
   has no names or metadata; a file system or a database lays out its own structures on it.
2. **File storage** presents named **files** in a directory tree. A file is a finite sequence of bytes that can be appended to and read or written
   at any offset; each directory stores the names, permissions and locations of its entries. **Network-attached storage** serves a file system to
   other machines over the network.
3. **Object storage** presents a flat map from **keys**, grouped in **buckets**, to immutable **objects**: an object is written once as a whole,
   read whole or by byte ranges, and changed only by writing a new object under its key. Listing the keys with a given prefix replaces listing a
   directory.
4. A **distributed file system** stores files on many machines: each file is split into large fixed-size **chunks**, each chunk is replicated on
   several **chunkservers**, and a **master** keeps the namespace and the map from files to chunks and from chunks to their locations. Clients ask
   the master for metadata and exchange data directly with the chunkservers.
:::

::::

Item 4 is the architecture of GFS: "A GFS cluster consists of a single master and multiple chunkservers", files are "divided into fixed-size
chunks", each "replicated on multiple chunkservers", and "clients interact with the master for metadata operations, but all data-bearing
communication goes directly to the chunkservers" [@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 2.3]. @fig-st-gfs draws it.

![The architecture of a distributed file system: the client asks the master for chunk locations, then reads and writes chunk data directly on
the chunkservers.](figures/gfs_architecture.svg){#fig-st-gfs width=85%}

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Reis and Housley define a file by three properties. Objects keep only the first.

::: {#exm-st-reis-file}
#### What a file is

A file has "finite length", supports "append operations" and "random access": "we can read from any location in the file or write updates to
any location"; "objects in object storage support only the first characteristic, finite length, but are still extremely useful"
[@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 6, pp. 199-200].
:::

A path is resolved one directory at a time. Each step reads a directory's metadata.

::: {#exm-st-path-lookup}
#### Resolving a path

For `/Users/matthewhousley/output.txt`, the operating system "starts at the root directory /, finds Users, matthewhousley, and finally
output.txt", looking "at the metadata at each hierarchy level" and following "the pointer to the next subdirectory"
[@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 6, p. 200]. The run resolves a path one component at a time in a temporary directory.

```{.python .run}
import os, tempfile
root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
os.makedirs(os.path.join(root, "Users", "matthewhousley"))
open(os.path.join(root, "Users", "matthewhousley", "output.txt"), "w").write("hello")
node = root
for part in ["Users", "matthewhousley", "output.txt"]:
    assert part in os.listdir(node)                     # read the directory's entries
    node = os.path.join(node, part); print("found", part)
print(open(node).read())
```

```{.text .run-output}
found Users
found matthewhousley
found output.txt
hello
```
:::

A block is the smallest unit a disk writes. Changing one byte rewrites a block.

::: {#exm-st-block}
#### Blocks

"A block is the smallest addressable unit of data supported by a disk. This was often 512 bytes ... but it has now grown to 4,096 bytes for most
current disks" [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 6, p. 202]. A database page is one or a few blocks, and "transactional databases still
rely on the high random access performance offered by direct access to a block storage device" (same page): updating one row rewrites at least
its block.
:::

An object can only be replaced. A few lines of Python model the interface of item 3.

::: {#exm-st-object-store}
#### An object store

"Objects don't support random writes or append operations; instead, they are written once as a stream of bytes ... To change data in an object or
append data to it, we must rewrite the full object" [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 6, p. 206].

```{.python .run}
class ObjectStore:
    def __init__(self):
        self.objects = {}
    def put(self, bucket, key, data: bytes):
        self.objects[(bucket, key)] = bytes(data)           # replaces the whole object
    def get(self, bucket, key, start=0, end=None):
        return self.objects[(bucket, key)][start:end]        # whole object or a byte range
    def list(self, bucket, prefix):
        return sorted(k for b, k in self.objects if b == bucket and k.startswith(prefix))
s = ObjectStore()
s.put("photos", "u42/2025/p1.jpg", b"\xff\xd8 jpeg bytes"); s.put("photos", "u42/2025/p2.jpg", b"\xff\xd8 more")
s.put("photos", "u42/2025/p1.jpg", s.get("photos", "u42/2025/p1.jpg") + b" appended")   # an append is a rewrite
print(s.list("photos", "u42/"), s.get("photos", "u42/2025/p1.jpg", 3, 7))
```

```{.text .run-output}
['u42/2025/p1.jpg', 'u42/2025/p2.jpg'] b'jpeg'
```
:::

Object stores have no directories. A listing filters keys.

::: {#exm-st-prefix-listing}
#### Listing a "directory"

For the key `project-data/11/23/2021/data.txt`, "the object system does not traverse a directory tree"; listing `project-data/11/` means that "the
object store must filter keys on the key prefix", and "if the bucket contains millions of objects, this operation might take some time, even if
the 'subdirectory' houses only a few objects" [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 6, p. 208].
:::

The photo service stores photos and metadata separately. Each goes where its access pattern fits.

::: {#exm-st-photoshare}
#### Photos in an object store

Photos of $2\,\mathrm{MB}$ (@exm-req-workload-assumptions) are written once and never changed, read whole or by range, and are far too many for one
machine: object storage. Their $1\,\mathrm{kB}$ of metadata is queried, joined and updated: a database on block storage, with the object key in
the `photos` row.
:::

The GFS master keeps all metadata in memory. The arithmetic shows why that is possible.

::: {#exm-st-gfs-metadata}
#### Metadata in memory

"The master maintains less than 64 bytes of metadata for each 64 MB chunk" [@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 2.6.1]. A petabyte is
$10^{15}/(6.4 \times 10^7) \approx 1.6 \times 10^7$ chunks, under $1\,\mathrm{GB}$ of metadata; with three replicas, the chunkservers hold
$3\,\mathrm{PB}$.

```{.python .run}
chunks = 1e15 / 64e6
print(f"{chunks:.2e} chunks, at most {chunks * 64 / 1e9:.2f} GB of chunk metadata")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1.56e+07 chunks, at most 1.00 GB of chunk metadata
```
:::

HDFS follows the same design. Tan summarises it.

::: {#exm-st-hdfs}
#### HDFS

"An HDFS cluster has an active NameNode, a passive (backup) NameNode, and multiple DataNode nodes"; the NameNode "determines the mapping of blocks to
DataNodes", "user data never flows through the NameNode", files are "divided into blocks, which are sharded across DataNode nodes", the default
block size is $64\,\mathrm{MB}$, and "HDFS is append-only, and does not support UPDATE or DELETE operations" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024,
Sec. 4.3.5, pp. 85-86]. NameNode, DataNode and HDFS block are GFS's master, chunkserver and chunk.
:::

GFS guarantees less than a local file system. Its consistency model names the outcomes.

::: {#exm-st-gfs-consistency}
#### Defined and undefined regions

"A file region is consistent if all clients will always see the same data, regardless of which replicas they read from. A region is defined after
a file data mutation if it is consistent and clients will see what the mutation writes in its entirety"; concurrent successful writes leave a region
"undefined but consistent", and "a failed mutation makes the region inconsistent" [@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 2.7.1]. A local file system, by
contrast, gives "full read after write consistency" [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 6, p. 201].
:::

Storage can be tiered by temperature. Liu calls the slow tier cold storage.

::: {#exm-st-cold}
#### Cold storage

"Recent data is usually accessed more frequently than past data. You can take advantage of that fact by moving data from hot storage to cold
storage", which is "usually cheaper to maintain", provided that "after you move the data, the performance constraints are still satisfied"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Cold Storage"]. Photos older than a year are rarely viewed and are candidates for a cheaper storage class of
the object store.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise matches data to storage. Each answer follows from the operations the data needs.

::: {#exr-st-choose}
#### Which storage?

Choose block, file or object storage for: the data files of the photo service's database; the photos; a configuration directory shared by a few
servers; the boot disk of a virtual machine; nightly database backups.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Database files: block storage, for random rewrites of pages. Photos: object storage, written once and read whole. Shared configuration: network-
attached file storage, small files edited in place by name. Boot disk: block storage, which Reis and Housley note "remains the default option for
operating system boot disks on cloud VMs" [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 6, p. 202]. Backups: object storage, written once, rarely read.

## Python

The choice as a rule on the operations needed.

```{.python .run}
needs = {"database files": {"random write"}, "photos": {"write once", "whole read"}, "shared config": {"names", "in-place edit", "shared"},
         "boot disk": {"random write", "boot"}, "backups": {"write once"}}
def choose(n):
    if "random write" in n: return "block"
    if "in-place edit" in n: return "file (NAS)"
    return "object"
for k, n in needs.items():
    print(f"{k:15s} -> {choose(n)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
database files  -> block
photos          -> object
shared config   -> file (NAS)
boot disk       -> block
backups         -> object
```
::::
:::

The second exercise prices appends on an object store. Each append rewrites the object.

::: {#exr-st-append-cost}
#### Appending to an object

A service appends $1000$ log lines of $100\,\mathrm{B}$ to a log that starts at $100\,\mathrm{MB}$. Compare the bytes written when the log is a file
and when it is one object; what key scheme avoids the cost?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The file is appended: $10^5\,\mathrm{B}$. The object is rewritten each time: about $1000 \times 100\,\mathrm{MB} = 100\,\mathrm{GB}$. Writing each
batch as a new object under a key such as `logs/2025-06-01/part-0001` makes every write a new object, and readers list the prefix.

## Python

The two totals.

```{.python .run}
start, line, n = 100e6, 100, 1000
file_bytes = n * line
object_bytes = sum(start + (i + 1) * line for i in range(n))
print(f"file {file_bytes:.0e} B, object {object_bytes:.3e} B, ratio {object_bytes / file_bytes:.0e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
file 1e+05 B, object 1.001e+11 B, ratio 1e+06
```
::::
:::

The third exercise sizes the GFS master for the photo service. The answer decides whether one master suffices.

::: {#exr-st-master-memory}
#### A master for the photos

Five years of photos at $2 \times 10^7$ a day, $2\,\mathrm{MB}$ each, are stored in a GFS-like file system with $64\,\mathrm{MB}$ chunks, packed into
large files. Estimate the master's chunk metadata, and the namespace if each photo were its own file at $64$ bytes per file.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The data is $3.65 \times 10^{10}$ photos, $7.3 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{B}$, or $1.1 \times 10^9$ chunks: about $73\,\mathrm{GB}$ of chunk metadata,
large but possible in memory. One file per photo adds $3.65 \times 10^{10} \times 64\,\mathrm{B} = 2.3\,\mathrm{TB}$ of namespace, which no single
master holds, and a chunk per photo would multiply the chunk count by $32$. Small objects need a different design, which is one reason object stores
exist.

## Python

The estimates.

```{.python .run}
photos = 2e7 * 365 * 5
data = photos * 2e6
chunks = data / 64e6
print(f"photos {photos:.2e}, data {data:.2e} B, chunks {chunks:.2e}, chunk metadata {chunks * 64 / 1e9:.0f} GB, "
      f"namespace one file per photo {photos * 64 / 1e12:.1f} TB")
```

```{.text .run-output}
photos 3.65e+10, data 7.30e+16 B, chunks 1.14e+09, chunk metadata 73 GB, namespace one file per photo 2.3 TB
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise weighs GFS's chunk size. Large chunks help the master and hurt small files.

::: {#exr-st-chunk-size}
#### The size of a chunk

GFS lists three advantages of $64\,\mathrm{MB}$ chunks and one disadvantage [@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 2.5]. For a client reading a $10\,\mathrm{GB}$
file sequentially, count the metadata requests with $64\,\mathrm{MB}$ and with $4\,\mathrm{MB}$ chunks, and explain the hot spot that a single-chunk
executable caused.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

At most one request per chunk: $157$ with $64\,\mathrm{MB}$ chunks, $2500$ with $4\,\mathrm{MB}$ (fewer, since the master returns locations for several
chunks at once). The advantages are fewer master interactions, persistent connections to a chunkserver, and less metadata; the disadvantage is that a
small file is one chunk on three chunkservers, which "were overloaded by hundreds of simultaneous requests" when hundreds of machines started the same
executable. GFS fixed it with a higher replication factor and staggered starts.

## Python

The request counts.

```{.python .run}
import math
for chunk in (64e6, 4e6):
    print(f"chunk {chunk / 1e6:.0f} MB: {math.ceil(10e9 / chunk)} chunk-location lookups")
```

```{.text .run-output}
chunk 64 MB: 157 chunk-location lookups
chunk 4 MB: 2500 chunk-location lookups
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise reconciles two statements about small files. Tan and GFS disagree on the space a small file takes.

::: {#exr-st-small-file-space}
#### Does a one-row file take a block?

Tan warns that "an INSERT query creates a new file with a single row, which will occupy an entire 64 MB block and is wasteful"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 4.3.5, p. 86], while GFS stores each chunk "as a plain Linux file" that "is extended only as needed", so that "lazy
space allocation avoids wasting space" [@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 2.5]. Which cost is real?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With lazy allocation a one-row file takes its own size on disk (times the replicas), not $64\,\mathrm{MB}$. The real cost is in the metadata: one file
name and one chunk entry at the master (or NameNode) per row, and Tan's following sentence, that such inserts contribute "to the number of names" and
exhaust the name quota, is the accurate part. Many small files load the master; few large files do not.

## Python

Disk and metadata for $10^6$ one-row files of $200\,\mathrm{B}$ against one file holding the same rows.

```{.python .run}
rows, size, meta = 10**6, 200, 64 + 64          # bytes per row; namespace plus chunk metadata per file
print(f"many files: disk {rows * size * 3 / 1e6:.0f} MB, master metadata {rows * meta / 1e6:.0f} MB")
print(f"one file:   disk {rows * size * 3 / 1e6:.0f} MB, master metadata {meta * 1} B")
```

```{.text .run-output}
many files: disk 600 MB, master metadata 128 MB
one file:   disk 600 MB, master metadata 128 B
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise computes the time to replicate a write. GFS pipelines the data along a chain.

::: {#exr-st-pipeline}
#### Pushing data to replicas

GFS states that "the ideal elapsed time for transferring B bytes to R replicas is B/T + RL" with $T = 100\,\mathrm{Mbps}$ and $L$ "far below 1 ms", so
"1 MB can ideally be distributed in about 80 ms" [@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 3.2]. Check the figure for $R = 3$ and compare with a client that sends the
data to each replica in turn from its one link.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$B/T = 8 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{b}/10^8\,\mathrm{b/s} = 80\,\mathrm{ms}$, plus $3L < 3\,\mathrm{ms}$. Sending to each replica from the client's link takes
$RB/T = 240\,\mathrm{ms}$: the chain uses each machine's full outbound link once instead of dividing the client's link among the recipients.

## Python

Both times with $L = 0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$.

```{.python .run}
B, T, L, R = 8e6, 1e8, 0.5e-3, 3
print(f"pipelined chain {1e3 * (B / T + R * L):.1f} ms; one after another {1e3 * R * B / T:.0f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
pipelined chain 81.5 ms; one after another 240 ms
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise handles the duplicates of record append. At least once means readers must deduplicate.

::: {#exr-st-record-append}
#### At least once

GFS's record append writes a record "at least once as an atomic unit", and a retried append can leave "duplicates of the same record"
[@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 3.3]. Simulate appends that fail after writing with probability $0.1$ and are retried, and show that a reader that skips
repeated record identifiers recovers each record exactly once.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A failed attempt may have written the record on some replicas, so the file can contain it more than once; the expected number of copies is
$1/(1 - 0.1) \approx 1.11$ when every failed attempt leaves a copy. A reader that cannot tolerate duplicates "can filter them out using unique
identifiers in the records" [@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 2.7.2], which the run does.

## Python

The appends and the deduplicating reader.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(16)
log = []
for rid in range(10_000):
    while True:
        log.append((rid, f"event {rid}"))            # the attempt writes the record
        if random.random() >= 0.1:                    # and reports success
            break
seen, out = set(), []
for rid, body in log:
    if rid not in seen:
        seen.add(rid); out.append(body)
print(f"records in file {len(log)}, copies per record {len(log) / 10_000:.3f}, after dedup {len(out)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
records in file 11104, copies per record 1.110, after dedup 10000
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise estimates the durability of three replicas. Independence is the assumption to question.

::: {#exr-st-replica-loss}
#### Losing all replicas

Each chunkserver disk fails independently with probability $q = 10^{-4}$ per day, and a lost replica is re-created within a day. Bound the probability
that a given chunk loses all three replicas on one day, and the expected number of chunks lost per year among $10^9$. Why is the true risk higher?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By [independence](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-independence), all three fail on the same day with
probability $q^3 = 10^{-12}$; over $365$ days and $10^9$ chunks the expected loss is $0.37$ chunks a year. Failures are not independent: replicas on one
rack share "a shared resource like a network switch or power circuit", which is why GFS must "spread chunk replicas across racks"
[@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 4.2], and a bad batch of disks fails together.

## Python

The numbers.

```{.python .run}
q, chunks = 1e-4, 1e9
print(f"per chunk-day {q**3:.0e}; expected chunks lost per year {q**3 * 365 * chunks:.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
per chunk-day 1e-12; expected chunks lost per year 0.37
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise applies GFS's consistency model to scenarios. Table 1 of the paper is the key.

::: {#exr-st-regions}
#### Classifying regions

Using @exm-st-gfs-consistency, classify the region after: (i) one client's write succeeds with no concurrent writer; (ii) two clients write the same
region concurrently and both succeed; (iii) a write fails at one secondary; (iv) a record append succeeds after one retry.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(i) Defined. (ii) Consistent but undefined: every replica holds the same bytes, mingled from both writes. (iii) Inconsistent: the replicas differ. (iv)
The region returned to the client is defined; the failed attempt may leave an inconsistent region or a duplicate elsewhere, "defined interspersed with
inconsistent" in the paper's table [@ghemawat2003google, Sec. 2.7.1].

## Python

Two concurrent writes applied in the same order on every replica, interleaved by chunk-sized pieces.

```{.python .run}
region = [None] * 8
writes = {"A": ["a"] * 8, "B": ["b"] * 8}
order = [("A", range(0, 4)), ("B", range(0, 8)), ("A", range(4, 8))]        # the primary's serial order of the pieces
replicas = []
for _ in range(3):
    r = list(region)
    for who, idx in order:
        for i in idx:
            r[i] = writes[who][i]
    replicas.append("".join(r))
print("replicas:", replicas, "| consistent:", len(set(replicas)) == 1, "| defined (one writer's data):", replicas[0] in ("a" * 8, "b" * 8))
```

```{.text .run-output}
replicas: ['bbbbaaaa', 'bbbbaaaa', 'bbbbaaaa'] | consistent: True | defined (one writer's data): False
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise designs object keys for the photo service. The key decides which listings are cheap.

::: {#exr-st-keys}
#### Keys for photos

Propose object keys for photos so that one user's photos can be listed by prefix, and say why `date/user/photo` is a worse choice for the profile page.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

`photos/u{user_id}/{photo_id}.jpg` puts a user's photos under one prefix, so the profile page lists `photos/u42/`. With `date/user/photo` a user's photos
are spread over every date prefix, and listing them filters all keys, the costly operation of @exm-st-prefix-listing. In practice the metadata database
answers "the photos of user 42" and the key is only stored, which removes the question.

## Python

The two layouts and the keys a listing must filter.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(17)
photos = [(random.randrange(1000), d, p) for p, d in enumerate(random.choices(range(365), k=50_000))]
by_user = sorted(f"photos/u{u}/{p}.jpg" for u, d, p in photos)
by_date = sorted(f"{d:03d}/u{u}/{p}.jpg" for u, d, p in photos)
mine_user = [k for k in by_user if k.startswith("photos/u42/")]
mine_date = [k for k in by_date if f"/u42/" in k]
print(f"user layout: {len(mine_user)} keys under one prefix; date layout: {len(mine_date)} keys spread over "
      f"{len({k[:3] for k in mine_date})} prefixes, found by scanning {len(by_date)} keys")
```

```{.text .run-output}
user layout: 56 keys under one prefix; date layout: 56 keys spread over 50 prefixes, found by scanning 50000 keys
```
::::
:::
::::

## Full-text search and inverted indexes {#sec-full-text-search}

The indexes of @sec-storage-engines find rows by the value of a column, or by a prefix of it. A search for the photos whose caption contains
"harbour" asks for something else, rows by a word anywhere in a text, and a B-tree on the caption cannot help: Tan's first technique,
`WHERE Lower(<column>) LIKE "%Lower(<search_term>)%"`, reads every row and "should only be used as a quick temporary implementation"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 2.6.1, p. 41]. Search engines invert the table instead: for each word they store the documents that contain it.
Liu calls full-text search "a pretty popular feature that is relevant to a lot of system design questions", such as "searching for images with
labels, tweets with text, and chat history with messages" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Full-Text Search"]. This section defines the
inverted index, its queries and its ranking, and runs them in SQLite's full-text extension FTS5.

For more on this topic, see @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Full-Text Search", and App. 5, "TF / IDF"], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024
[Ch. 11, "Data flow and indexing" and "Relevance scoring and ranking"], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 2.6] and @sqliteFTS5.

### Inverted indexes, queries and ranking

An inverted index is built from terms, not from raw text: the text is first reduced to a sequence of terms by the steps Liu lists, and the index
maps each term to the documents in which it occurs. We write $\mathcal D$ for the collection of documents, $|\mathcal D|$ for their number and
$|d|$ for the number of terms of a document $d$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-inverted-index}
#### Inverted index, posting lists and tf-idf

1. An **analyser** maps a text to a sequence of **terms** by **normalising** it (lower case, punctuation removed), **tokenising** it into words,
   removing **stop words** that occur in almost every text, and **stemming** each word to a common stem.
2. The **inverted index** of $\mathcal D$ maps each term $t$ to its **posting list**: the identifiers of the documents containing $t$, in increasing
   order, each optionally with the **positions** at which $t$ occurs. The **document frequency** $\mathrm{df}_t$ is the length of the posting list,
   and the **term frequency** $\mathrm{tf}_{t,d}$ is the number of occurrences of $t$ in $d$.
3. A **Boolean query** combines terms with AND, OR and NOT and is answered by intersecting, uniting and subtracting posting lists. A **phrase query**
   for $t_1 t_2 \cdots t_j$ matches the documents in which the terms occur at consecutive positions.
4. A **ranking function** assigns a score to each matching document. The **tf-idf** score of $d$ for a query $q$ is
   $$
   \operatorname{tfidf}(d, q) = \sum_{t \in q}\mathrm{tf}_{t,d}\,\ln\frac{|\mathcal D|}{\mathrm{df}_t},
   $$
   the sum over the query's terms that occur in the collection.
:::

::::

The tf-idf formula is the chapter's convention: Liu describes the idea, that "the more frequent the word exists and the rarer it exists across the
documents, the higher the score is" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 5, "TF / IDF"], and Sinha names it as one factor of Elasticsearch's
scoring [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 11, "Relevance scoring and ranking"], but neither gives a formula, and several variants are in use.
SQLite ranks with BM25, a refinement given below.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Liu's four steps turn a caption into terms. A few lines of Python implement them.

::: {#exm-ii-analyser}
#### An analyser

Liu's steps are: "Change uppercase to lowercase and remove special characters", "Split the full text into tokens", remove stop words since "words like
'the' and 'for' exist in all documents", and stem, "like 'studying' to 'study'" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Full-Text Search"]. The run
uses a crude suffix-stripping stemmer.

```{.python .run}
import re
STOP = {"the", "a", "at", "for", "of", "over", "and", "on", "in"}
def stem(w):
    for suffix in ("ing", "ies", "es", "s", "ed"):
        if w.endswith(suffix) and len(w) - len(suffix) >= 3:
            return w[: -len(suffix)] + ("y" if suffix == "ies" else "")
    return w
def analyse(text):
    words = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9 ]", " ", text.lower()).split()
    return [stem(w) for w in words if w not in STOP]
print(analyse("Studying the Boats at the Harbour -- sunsets!"))
```

```{.text .run-output}
['study', 'boat', 'harbour', 'sunset']
```
:::

Building the index is one pass over the documents. Posting lists come out sorted when documents are added in order.

::: {#exm-ii-build}
#### Building an inverted index

Three captions of the photo service give the index below; "for each token, the database will store a list of documents called a posting", and "the
posting list is sorted by specific attributes such an ID or ranking score" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Full-Text Search"].

```{.python .run}
from collections import defaultdict
captions = {1: "sunset over the harbour", 2: "boats in the harbour at night", 3: "night market"}
index = defaultdict(list)
for doc_id in sorted(captions):
    for pos, term in enumerate(captions[doc_id].split()):
        if term not in {"the", "over", "in", "at"}:
            if not index[term] or index[term][-1][0] != doc_id:
                index[term].append((doc_id, []))
            index[term][-1][1].append(pos)
for term in sorted(index):
    print(f"{term:8s} -> {index[term]}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
boats    -> [(2, [0])]
harbour  -> [(1, [3]), (2, [3])]
market   -> [(3, [1])]
night    -> [(2, [5]), (3, [0])]
sunset   -> [(1, [0])]
```
:::

A two-word phrase can be indexed as a term. Liu calls it an n-gram.

::: {#exm-ii-bigram}
#### Bigrams

Since "system design" and "San Francisco" have meaning together, an index of 2-grams lets a search for "system design" find the documents directly;
"the trade-off is extra storage since there are more keys to store" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "N-Gram"]. A document of $|d|$ terms has
$|d| - 1$ bigrams, so the index roughly doubles in size.
:::

Boolean queries are set operations on posting lists. AND is an intersection.

::: {#exm-ii-boolean}
#### Boolean queries

With the index of @exm-ii-build, "harbour AND night" intersects $[1, 2]$ and $[2, 3]$, "harbour OR night" unites them, and "night AND NOT harbour"
subtracts. Liu notes that "system design" might mean "system AND design", "system OR design" or the phrase, so the interface must say which
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Search Query"].

```{.python .run}
post = {"harbour": [1, 2], "night": [2, 3]}
print("AND", sorted(set(post["harbour"]) & set(post["night"])), "| OR", sorted(set(post["harbour"]) | set(post["night"])),
      "| AND NOT", sorted(set(post["night"]) - set(post["harbour"])))
```

```{.text .run-output}
AND [2] | OR [1, 2, 3] | AND NOT [3]
```
:::

SQLite's FTS5 provides an inverted index as a virtual table. Its query operator is `MATCH`.

::: {#exm-ii-fts5}
#### FTS5

An FTS5 table answers queries for documents that contain terms, "phrases - sequences of terms or prefix terms that must feature in a document", and
terms within a given distance ("NEAR queries") [@sqliteFTS5, Sec. 1]. With the porter tokenizer, "search terms like 'correction'" match "similar words
such as 'corrected' or 'correcting'" [@sqliteFTS5, Sec. 4.3.3].

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE captions USING fts5(caption, tokenize = porter)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO captions(rowid, caption) VALUES (?, ?)",
               [(1, "Sunset over the harbour"), (2, "Boats in the harbour at night"), (3, "Night market"), (4, "Sailing boats")])
for q in ("harbour AND night", "harbour OR market", '"harbour at night"', "boat", "sail*"):
    print(f"{q:20s}", [r[0] for r in db.execute("SELECT rowid FROM captions WHERE captions MATCH ? ORDER BY rowid", (q,))])
```

```{.text .run-output}
harbour AND night    [2]
harbour OR market    [1, 2, 3]
"harbour at night"   [2]
boat                 [2, 4]
sail*                [4]
```
:::

A `LIKE` pattern with a leading wildcard reads every row. The query plan shows it.

::: {#exm-ii-like-scan}
#### Why not `LIKE`?

Tan's first technique lacks "sophisticated features like boosting, weight, fuzzy search, or text preprocessing such as stemming or tokenization"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 2.6.1, p. 41], and it is slow: a B-tree index orders captions by their beginning, so `LIKE '%harbour%'` is a SCAN
of the table.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE photos(photo_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, caption TEXT)"); db.execute("CREATE INDEX by_caption ON photos(caption)")
print([r[-1] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT photo_id FROM photos WHERE caption LIKE '%harbour%'")])
```

```{.text .run-output}
['SCAN photos']
```
:::

Liu's example compares two documents. Only one term distinguishes them.

::: {#exm-ii-liu-tfidf}
#### Liu's tf-idf example

For "Document A: 'please study system design'" and "Document B: 'please study system design interview'", "when someone searches for 'interview,'
document B has a higher number for 'interview,' hence should score higher" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 5, "TF / IDF"]. With item 4,
"interview" has $\mathrm{df} = 1$ and idf $\ln 2$; the four shared terms have idf $\ln 1 = 0$ and contribute nothing.

```{.python .run}
import math
docs = {"A": "please study system design".split(), "B": "please study system design interview".split()}
df = {t: sum(t in d for d in docs.values()) for d in docs.values() for t in d}
for q in ("interview", "system design"):
    print(q, {k: round(sum(d.count(t) * math.log(len(docs) / df[t]) for t in q.split()), 3) for k, d in docs.items()})
```

```{.text .run-output}
interview {'A': 0.0, 'B': 0.693}
system design {'A': 0.0, 'B': 0.0}
```
:::

SQLite's ranking function is BM25. Its documentation gives the formula.

::: {#exm-ii-bm25}
#### BM25 in SQLite

FTS5's `bm25()` returns, for a document $d$ and a query with phrases $q_i$,
$$
-\sum_i \mathrm{IDF}(q_i)\,\frac{f(q_i, d)\,(k_1 + 1)}{f(q_i, d) + k_1\big(1 - b + b\,|d|/\overline{|d|}\big)}, \qquad \mathrm{IDF}(q_i) = \log\frac{|\mathcal
D| - n(q_i) + 0.5}{n(q_i) + 0.5},
$$
where $f(q_i, d)$ is the phrase frequency, $n(q_i)$ the number of rows containing the phrase, $\overline{|d|}$ the average number of tokens, and
"k1 and b are both constants, hard-coded at 1.2 and 0.75 respectively"; the sign is reversed so that "better matches are assigned numerically lower
scores" and `ORDER BY bm25(ft)` lists the best first [@sqliteFTS5, Sec. 5.1.1]. Compared with tf-idf, the term frequency saturates (the fraction is
below $k_1 + 1$) and long documents are penalised.
:::

FTS5 stores its index as several b-trees that are merged. That is an LSM tree.

::: {#exm-ii-fts5-merge}
#### An LSM tree of b-trees

"Each time a new transaction is committed, a new b-tree containing the contents of the committed transaction is written into the database file. When
the full-text index is queried, each b-tree must be queried individually and the results merged", and "smaller b-trees are periodically merged into
single larger b-trees" [@sqliteFTS5, Sec. 6.1]; in its contentless-delete tables a deleted row gets a "tombstone" marker, and "when the b-tree is merged with other b-trees, both the deleted
rows and their tombstone markers are discarded" [@sqliteFTS5, Sec. 6.5]. This is item
3 of @def-storage-engine with b-trees in place of SSTables.
:::

Sinha's Twitter design indexes tweets as they are created. The index is kept fresh by events.

::: {#exm-ii-sinha-flow}
#### Indexing as data arrives

"When a new tweet is created, Tweet Service sends the tweet data to Search Service", which extracts "the text content, hashtags, mentions, and user
details", and "the extracted data is then indexed in Elasticsearch, creating an inverted index that maps terms to tweet IDs"
[@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 11, "Data flow and indexing"]. The photo service can index captions the same way at upload; Liu adds that
"based on freshness, you may decide to index every day or every minute" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Full-Text Search"].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves the merge that answers AND queries. Sortedness makes it linear.

::: {#exr-ii-intersection}
#### Intersecting posting lists

Two sorted lists $A$ and $B$ without repeats are intersected by advancing a pointer in each: if the two current values are equal, output it and advance
both, otherwise advance the pointer at the smaller value. Prove that the result is $A \cap B$ in increasing order after at most $|A| + |B| - 1$
comparisons.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Invariant: every common element not yet output lies at or after both pointers. It holds at the start. If the current values are equal, the value is
common and is output, and advancing both keeps the invariant. If $a_i < b_j$, then $a_i$ is not in $B$: every element of $B$ before $b_j$ was passed
because it was smaller than some $a_{i'} \leq a_i$ and $B$ is increasing, so $a_i \notin B$, and skipping it loses nothing. Output values increase
because both pointers only move forward. Each comparison advances at least one pointer, and the loop stops when one list is exhausted, so it makes at
most $|A| + |B| - 1$ comparisons.

## Python

The merge, checked against set intersection, with a comparison count.

```{.python .run}
import random
def intersect(a, b):
    i = j = comps = 0; out = []
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        comps += 1
        if a[i] == b[j]:
            out.append(a[i]); i += 1; j += 1
        elif a[i] < b[j]:
            i += 1
        else:
            j += 1
    return out, comps
random.seed(18)
for _ in range(1000):
    a, b = sorted(random.sample(range(200), random.randrange(1, 60))), sorted(random.sample(range(200), random.randrange(1, 60)))
    out, comps = intersect(a, b)
    assert out == sorted(set(a) & set(b)) and comps <= len(a) + len(b) - 1
print("1000 random pairs: correct, within |A| + |B| - 1 comparisons")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1000 random pairs: correct, within |A| + |B| - 1 comparisons
```
::::
:::

The second exercise merges many lists for an OR query. Liu names the algorithm.

::: {#exr-ii-merge-k}
#### Merging $k$ lists

Liu suggests merging posting lists "using the merge k list algorithm since the posting lists are sorted already" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020,
Ch. 5, "Search Query"]. Prove that a heap of the $k$ current heads unites $k$ sorted lists of total length $L$ in $O(L\log k)$ time, and run it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The heap holds at most one element per list, the current head. Popping the minimum gives the smallest remaining element of all lists, since each
list's remaining elements are at least its head; pushing that list's next element restores the property. Each of the $L$ elements is pushed and popped
once, at $O(\log k)$ per heap operation. Skipping an output equal to the previous one removes duplicates for OR.

## Python

`heapq.merge` implements the heap merge.

```{.python .run}
import heapq
lists = [[1, 4, 9], [2, 4, 10, 12], [3, 9]]
out = []
for x in heapq.merge(*lists):
    if not out or out[-1] != x:
        out.append(x)
print(out)
```

```{.text .run-output}
[1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12]
```
::::
:::

The third exercise orders the lists of a long AND query. The smallest list bounds the work.

::: {#exr-ii-smallest-first}
#### Smallest list first

For an AND of $k$ terms, prove that the result has at most $\min_i\mathrm{df}_{t_i}$ documents, and that intersecting in increasing order of
document frequency keeps every intermediate result no larger than the smallest list. Count the binary searches of both orders on lists of very different lengths.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

An intersection is contained in each of its operands, so its size is at most the smallest. Starting with the smallest list, each intermediate result
is an intersection that includes it, so its size is at most that list's. With the merge of @exr-ii-intersection each step costs the size of the
intermediate result plus the next list; with a search into the next list instead of a merge, a small intermediate makes each step cheaper still.

## Python

Three lists of very different lengths, intersected in both orders by searching each element of the intermediate result in the next list.

```{.python .run}
import random, bisect
random.seed(19)
lists = [sorted(random.sample(range(10**6), n)) for n in (300_000, 30_000, 300)]
def member(x, a):
    i = bisect.bisect_left(a, x); return i < len(a) and a[i] == x
def run(order):
    acc = lists[order[0]]; searches = 0
    for i in order[1:]:
        searches += len(acc); acc = [x for x in acc if member(x, lists[i])]
    return len(acc), searches
for order in ((0, 1, 2), (2, 1, 0)):
    n, searches = run(order)
    print(f"order by size {[len(lists[i]) for i in order]}: result {n}, binary searches {searches}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
order by size [300000, 30000, 300]: result 1, binary searches 308981
order by size [300, 30000, 300000]: result 1, binary searches 308
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise answers phrase queries with positions. Item 3's definition is the test.

::: {#exr-ii-phrase}
#### Phrase queries

Using a positional index, answer the phrase "harbour at night" on the captions of @exm-ii-fts5 without stop-word removal, and check against FTS5.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Intersect the posting lists of the three terms, then keep a document if some position $p$ of "harbour" has "at" at $p + 1$ and "night" at $p + 2$. Only
document 2 qualifies. Removing "at" as a stop word would break the phrase, which is why phrase search keeps positions of all words or indexes stop
words anyway.

## Python

The positional test.

```{.python .run}
from collections import defaultdict
docs = {1: "sunset over the harbour", 2: "boats in the harbour at night", 3: "night market", 4: "sailing boats"}
pos = defaultdict(dict)
for d, text in docs.items():
    for p, t in enumerate(text.split()):
        pos[t].setdefault(d, set()).add(p)
phrase = "harbour at night".split()
cands = set.intersection(*(set(pos[t]) for t in phrase))
hits = [d for d in sorted(cands) if any(all(p + i in pos[t][d] for i, t in enumerate(phrase)) for p in pos[phrase[0]][d])]
print("phrase matches", hits)
```

```{.text .run-output}
phrase matches [2]
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise sizes the caption index of the photo service. Postings are as many as tokens.

::: {#exr-ii-index-size}
#### The size of the caption index

Captions average $8$ terms after analysis, and $2 \times 10^7$ photos are uploaded a day. Estimate the postings after five years and the index size at
$4$ bytes per posting without positions, and compare with the captions' text at $50$ bytes each.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$3.65 \times 10^{10}$ photos give about $2.9 \times 10^{11}$ postings (repeated terms within a caption are rare), $1.2\,\mathrm{TB}$ at $4$ bytes,
against $1.8\,\mathrm{TB}$ of text: the index is the same order of size as the data, which is why it is compressed and sharded.

## Python

The estimate.

```{.python .run}
photos = 2e7 * 365 * 5
postings = photos * 8
print(f"photos {photos:.2e}, postings {postings:.2e}, index {postings * 4 / 1e12:.1f} TB, text {photos * 50 / 1e12:.1f} TB")
```

```{.text .run-output}
photos 3.65e+10, postings 2.92e+11, index 1.2 TB, text 1.8 TB
```
